It wasn't in this case: "Speaking of fishing experiences," .said the man in the neglige shirt, "I shall never -forget the day when Bob White and I—you kuow 'Bob ?—were trying our luck on Lake Squam. We had fished for an hour or more and had caughtionly a few little fellows, when suddenly I had an awful bite. "And you pulled in your line, hand over 'band, only to lose a ten-pound pickerel just as you were about to land kim," interrupted the fat man sitting on the flour barrel. THE SUNDERED HEARTS
OR, A WAR OF THE HOUSEHOLD.
By the Author of "The Double Life.' "The Bailiff's Scheme," &c., &c.
CHAPTER XXIII. A SUDDEN REVERSE.
For a momenti Dora, standing on the steps of the Coningsby mansion, was paralyzed by the peril which had overtaken her.

Jack Narr, with his sinister smile of exultation, continued to stand below her, with arms out- stretched, cutting off her retreat. "Come on, Miss Dora !" he exclaimed, his manner half respectful, half menacing. "You needn't be afraid of me! I won't harm you! I've a cab waiting around the corner, and you shall go home like a lady !" Dora looked around her like a frightened deer. There was a slight movement about the door of the cab in which Squire Weir awaited her. It seemed as if the young squire were about to alight. Narr's glances follows" hers. "Your cab, eh ?" he demanded. "I noticed it afore. The cabman can't help you, Miss Dora. You're booked to go home with me. Will you go peaceable, or shall we have a row? I can call a Bobby, and say as how I 'm your parent, and you're a runaway daughter, as has got sot up above her kin by being 'dopted out. The law is on my side. Coming ?" He came up a step nearer to her. At the same moment the young squire stepped out of the cab upon the pavement, and turned his face toward her.
Asudden inspiration—it was quicker than thought —seized Dora.
With the rapidity of a flash, she sprang down the steps, hurling Narr aside in her impetuous descent, and flew like a deer along the pavement toward the cab.

Narr recovered himself, and, with a wild oath, sprang in pursuit. The girl's superior lightness and fleetness won the day. The young squire, comprehending the situation, hurried to meet her, helped her into the cab, sprang in himself, and the vehicle rolled away, turning out of the square at the very moment that Narr came up to the spot where it had so long waited. The man's anger and fury can be imagined. He heaped imprecations upon the heads of both Dora and her friend, swore "to have the law on them both," and fairly raved in his disappointment, spending several precious minutes thus vainly before it occurred to him to call his cab and hasten in pursuit. When he had once conceived that idea, however, he hastened to put it into execution. A few minutes thereafter he was hurrying in the wake of Dora and the young squire, urging his cabman to make a desperate effort to overtake them.

Meanwhile Dora, pale and panting, leaned back in her vehicle, her hands trembling in the warm, reassuring clasp of Squire Weir. "Courage, Dora," said the young man, reas- suringly. "Ho cannot overtake us. See how fast we are going. Have faith in me. I will protect you, Dora. I will not let you go back to the Narrs."
A tremulous smile of gratitude, like a ray of sun- light, beamed from Dora's sorrowing young face. She drew a little nearer her lover.

"0, Noel !" she exclaimed, piteously, "I have no friend now but you. He—Jack Narr—looked terrible to me as he stood there to intercept me— more terrible than a wild beast! I can have no home with him and his. And Miss Coningsby has refused to assist me in any way unless I return to —to them !" and she shuddered. " What shall I do, Noel?" . . .

;`-l'he first thing to be done is to proceed to your new lodgings," replied Noel, cheerfully. "Leave it all to me, Dora. I will look after y,:ur future, my little sister." fie spoke the final words as if they cost him an effort. Dora flushed, then paled, and drew her hands from his; her sweet face gathering a deeper gravity and anxiety. "Noel," she sid, gravely, after a pause, during which she listened intently for the sound of pursu- ing wheels, failing to hear them, "you are very good to me—but lam not your sister I Miss Con- ingsby said it was improper for me to depend upon you for aid or counsel—" "Would it be better for you to be friendless, Dora ?" asked her lover, in a tender reproach. "I shall never forget the respect due to you, and to your isolation and trouble. But surely no one could find fault with you for accepting the simplest brotherly attentions from one who has known you from your earliest childhood—from one who was Squire Chessom's intimate and trusted friend? As soon as I have seen you safely placed, I will leave you; but not till then 1" "Can I not get a situation as a governess ?" suggested Dora. "The papers are full of adver- tisements, some of which might apply to me. My wants are humble enough, Noel. lam willing to do any honest labour, in any quiet position." It trembled upon the young squire's tongue to ask her again to become his wife, and allow him to protect and care for her, but it seemed to his generous soul like taking advantage of her desola- tion and helplessness, and he was silent. "Not yet 11 he said to himself. "I must wait until she has gotten over her disappointment about Felix Warner. Perhaps her heart may turn to me yet. I must wait." He sighed. Somehow such a happiness in reserve seemed improbable. In due time the cab arrived at the address Noel had given, and the young squire assisted Dora to alight. They found themselves in a quiet, respectable street, in that part of Notting Hill bordering on Kensington, and but a few minutes' walk from the Kensington Gardens. "We are at a safe distance from Lowater Cres- cent—as ale as if we were at the other end of London," said Noel. He swept a glance up and down the street, to see if they had been closely pursued, and then conducted Dora up the steps of a quiet, red-brick house in the middle of the block, and sounded the knocker loudly. A servant appearing, the young pair were ush- ered into a stuffy little parlour, and left for a few minutes to themselves. - -

"I believe I'll dismiss the cab," said the young man, looking from the window. "I know that Narr pursued us but I think he lost us somewhere in the crowd. 'Yet, to make sure, I'll send our cab away; so that, should he happen into this street, he will find no trace of us." He hastened to do so, going out for the purpose. When he returned, the landlady, Mrs. Box, made her appearance. She was a prim, severe-looking woman, a widow, and one of that innumerable class who "have seen better days." She wore a black dress and a widow's cap, and might have served as a model for a painter's inclrnation of Respectability, she was so cold, so staid, and so severe.

Her countenance evinced her surprise at seeing the young squire so accompanied. He had ob- served her sign of Apartments to Let, and had called that morning and engaged her drawing. room floor, consisting of two rooms, promising to take possession of them in the evening. The landlady treated him coldly, glancing in- quiringly at Dora. "Your sister, Mr. Weir r she asked.

"Not my shier, but a young lady from Sussex, the orphaned daughter of a late neighbour of mine," explained Noel. "I wish to resign my rooms in youi house to her, Mrs. Dox." The landlady's face hardened. She pursed up her mouth primly. "I regret, Mr. Weir," she said, "that I cannot accommodate your friend. If you choose to give up your rochns, you are at liberty to do so, but you cannot let them to another." Dora put back her veil, and lifted her pale, plead- ing face to the gaze of the landlady. That face, so pure, so child-like, so lovely, made an instant impression on Mrs. Dox. "If you refuse to receive me, madam, of course I must go," said the girl, in her sweet, troubled voice. But first let me tell you how much I need such a shelter as this house would be." "Yes, tell her, Dora," said Squire Weir, begin- ning to fear-that he should have to take his young charge to a hotel, and so expose her to the publicity from which she shrank.

Dora told her story in her impetuous, girlish way. Before she had finished she had won the heart of the landlady, for there waN a warm heart under all that buckram and armour of staid severity. "You shall stay," said Mrs. Pox, her face "You shall have Mr. Weir's rooms, and I will watch over you myself. It would be too great a shame if you should be comp:Med to go back to thee atrocious people. And I dare say I can find you some music scholars." Dora's eyes glowed, and her face lighted up with a sudden splendour.

She caught the landlady's hand in hers, pressing it warmly. "Poor young thing !" said Mrs. Dox, completely won now: "She 's just like a babe in the wood, Mr. Weir/ You can depend upon me, sir, to pro- tect her."

Weir's look of gratitude considerably enlightened the landlady as to his state of feeling toward Dora. She comprehended that he was Dora's lover, and a sort of maternal feeling toward them both took possession of her heart. Dora was taken upstairs and installed into her two rooms, a parlour and a bed-chamber connect- ing. Both were Edry, pleasant, and well furnished, and there was an air of neatness about them not common to lodging-houses in general. Dora made herself at home here at once, laying off her hat and sacque, and inviting Noel and Mr. Dox to be seated.

Both complied with the invitation. "Pity Miss Chessom was obliged to leave her boxes 1" observed the landlady, compassionately. "Can't they be got, Mr. Weir ?" "No. They will have to be given up, at least for the present," replied the young man. "Miss Chessom will be obliged to shop for a new ward- robe. It IA ill only endanger her liberty to go back to Lowater Crescent."
This view of the case was so evidently practical that Dora and Mrs. Dox resigned all thought of attempting to recover the abandoned effects of the former.

Presently Mrs. Dox withdrew for a few minutes, having a call below, and Noel arose to take his de- parture. "You must send for me if you need me, Dora," he said, taking her hand. "1 ihall call, in any case, to•morrow." _ _

"And by to-morrow I hope to be settled into my groove," replied Dora, Braille.% "If Mrs. Dox can get me pupils in music, I Elan not have longer need to tax your friendship, Noel. But, however independent I may become, I shall never cease to be grateful to you for all your goodness to me."

Noel's handsome face became yet more grave. " Do not speak of gratitude to me, Dora," he said, gently. "And now, good-bye for to-day." He lifted her hand to his lips with a chivalrous courtesy, and then went out from her presence, descending to the street. Dora looked after him from her window, with a sweet, steady smile curving her lips, and with a bright glow in her dusky eyes. "I wonder if he will ever ask me that question again ?" she thought, blushing. "How foolish I was! I wonder if he wants my love now? Yet, if he were to ask me again. I would not n:arry him. He would think I acce!)ted him riot frin love but for a.home. How noble an i grand he is ! And a pobr little fool I was to fling away the priceless gem for the worthless paste ! " She drew a sobbing sigh, and the tears came and dimmed the bright glow of her eyes, and .tne sweet smile quavered and became a pitiful sort of smile, indeed.
The remainder of the day—it wls now nearly dusk—and the evening passed drearily enough to Dora.

The next morning Mrs. Dux went out with the young girl, and procured for her two music pupils and the hope of more. In the afternoon Squire Weir called, and was informed of Dora's successes, the young girl assum- ing a very pretty air of independence, which quite enchanted her lover.

The young squire had also some news to com- municate. He had learned that Felix Warner had gone back to Norfolk, having been summoned by his relative, Lord Ohampney. "So there's nothing to fear from him, Dora," he said. "Nor from the Narrs either. They will be quite helpless to find you." The thought was comforting, but it was scarcely true. Jack Narr had been duly instructed by Warner, and was likely to prove a formidable enemy in the end.

Tit; young squire made a long call, and went away, promising to teturn again on the morrow. About an hour after his departure—toward dusk —when Mrs. Dox and Dora were in the midst of a discussion in the girl's parlour, a ring was heard. and presently the tramp of feet sounded on the stairs.

Dora rose to fly. "It's some one to see the third pair back," said Mrs. Dox. "He's an artist, and his friends are noisy. Don't be afraid, Miss—" At this juncture the door was burst open. Dora uttered a cry of alarm. At the same instant three persons came noisily into the room—Mrs. Narr, red and frowsy, her black bonnet bent awry, Jack Narr, also red-faced and jubilant, and a police officer, whose mental was greatly subordinate to his physical strength. "Here she is ! " cried Mrs. Narr, exultantly, pointing at the shrinking girl. "Here she is, sir, my own daughter, and the most ungrateful one that ever breathe.' ! Oh, you viper she ejacu- lated, shaking her hand at Dora. You ran away from es, did you? You upset your own pa on to the stone steps, did yoa " "A pretty way you treated me, Miss Dora!" said Jack Narr. If it hadn't been for follering Mr. Weir, we'd never knowed where you was ! "This is the young woman, then ? " asked the policeman. " Exactly( " said Narr, tilting himself on his toes and heels, in a state of blissful satisfaction. "She's the very piece of dimity, my fine Bobby!" "Do you deny that these people are your parents, my dear ? " asked the officer. "No—but--"

" Thatlt do. Put your bunnit on and go 'long of your mother," commanded the policeman, with an air of authority, determined to earn the golden sovereign Mrs. Narr had promised him for his services on this occasion. "No words, Miss. 'Long with you. The law gives the parent control of the child till she is of age. Will you go, or shall I take you afore a justice ? " Complaint and protestation were alike useless. Mrs. Dox dared not resist a policeman in uniform, and fell to weeping bitterly and wishing that Mr. Weir were time.

And Dora—poor, helpless Dora She was like a bird in the snare. She sat down, half stunned by this terrible reverse, and Mrs. Narr tied on her hat and put on her sacque. Then Jack Narr helped her down stairs, put her into the cab which was waiting, dismissed the stout policeman, and the cab drove away, with Dora seated between her two exulting enemies.
CHAPTER XXIV. THE_ NARRS. MAKE A DISCOVERY.

It was not in Dora.'s nature to --c-oh-t.int;e long In the gloom of her terrible despair, notwithstanding the titter misery of her situation. And soon, as she sat down in the moving cab, between her two enemies, she began to cast about in her own soul for a few beams of hope, as a plant in a dark cellar creeps towards a stray beam of light. She supposed, as a matter of course, that she was to be taken back to Lowater Crescent, there to be kept under the close guardianship of the Narrs. "It will go hard with me if I don't escape from them again,' she thought, kindling with a sudden resolution. "Noel will not abandon me! He will be at the Crescent to-morrow, as soon as possible after he learns of my disappearance. Dear Noel ! he is the only friead I have in all the wide world now !"

The thought that the young squire would not forsake her in her need comforted her like an abso- lute promise of help. Her eyes brightened, and a sudden glow lit up her sorrowing young face. "Perking up, hey ?" observed Jack Narr, in his jauntiest style. "Glad! to see it, Miss Dora. No need of your putting on airs, if you are somebody. You see, Miss Dora-"
" ' Miss Dora,' again, to your own daughter !" intcrrupted Mrs. Narr, harshly. "Anybody 'd think you was speaking to a superior, Jack Narr !"
"A superior! . Well, aint Lir

"Are -you ? ' demanded his wife, with a quick savage gleam in her eyes, and a sudden scowl upon her visage. "Be you crazy, Jack Narr, or be you a dowright fool ?" Narr started, his red face deepening in its colour- ing to crimson.

7` Don't be so hard on a fellow, old woman," he exclaimed, half humbly, half defiantly. "The gal's edicated, and I aint. She's been brought up a lady, looks like a lady, and dresses like a lady, and half the time I forget that she belongs to us. No harm's done. The gal knows that she's our daughter; don't you, now, Miss Dora ?" The remembrance of Squire Chessom's words came back to Dora—his doubts if she .really be- longed to these people. She answered Narr hastily and impulsively: "No, I don't know that I am your daughter, Mr. Narr! I have no evidence of any such fact, beyond your word and that ot your wife, and I have no faith whatever in your assurances !" Jack Narr eyed the young girl in stupid amaze- ment.

Mrs. Narr caught her breath with a quick gasp, and her face grew ashy pale, and a strange expres- sion gathered about her compressed mouth "Well, I never !" said Narr, stupidly. "So you think you aint our child ?' demanded Mrs. Narr, grimly. "And who may your royal highness be, then ?"

-I'l do not know who I am," responded Dora, looking drearily from the cab window into the gas- lit streets. "All I know is what my instinct tells me—that I am not of your blood !" "You couldn't give us no idea of who you are, now ?" sneered Mrs. Narr, bending nearer, and looking into the girl's wan face. " Aint you a Princess in disguise? What! you haven't no idea of who you are, even though you cast off your own flesh and blood through being ashamed of 'ern ?" •.)

"I could never be ashamed of honest kindred, however poor they might be," said Dora, sorrow- fully. "But you have not shown toward me the feelings of parents. You have acted like people who have become possessed of a prize which they hardly know how to manage. I know, in my own soul, that I a_n not your child. I may be the child whom you took to nurse with your own while you lived on your Surrey farm.' - Jack Narr uttered a quick exclamation. His wife caught her breath again sharply. "Stop where you are, Dora 1" the said, threat- eningly. "Not another word of such talk. You are our child, and the sooner you make up your mind to be dutiful and submissive, the better for you. As to your being our nurse-child,", she added, defiantly, "just prove it—that's all 1" Dora sighed and moved further away from Mrs. Narr. Jack transferred his bulky person to the opposite seat.
_ _ "I don't see how the gal could have got any such idea, old woman,' he observed, uneasily,
- "The least said the soonest mended 1" inter- rupted Nrs. Narr, warningly. - Her husband sank back silenced.

Not one of the three spoke again for many minutes. The cab rolled on through gas-lit streets, lined with quiet houses or gay shops, and Dora pressed her face against the window and looked out, with eyes that brimmed over with a great woe.

At last, as they bowled through the Strand, and turned down Wellington-street towards the river, Dora aroused herself to the fact that she was in a strange quarter. " Where are we ?" she asked, in a quick, startled tone. "We are not at Notting Hill. Are we not going back to Lowater Crescent ?"

"No. London don't agree with Jack and me," said Mrs. Narr, cooliy. "We aint town•bred folks. We're going down into the country a bit. There was a cottage to let on the Terns, and we've took it. The luggage went down this afternoon."

"This 'ere's Waterloo Bridge," explained Narr, as the cab rolled p,st the toll-house and entered on the bridge. "We'll soon be at Waterloostation, and the rest of the journey 'II be easy." Dora received this news with dismay. "Why are you going into the country, if you want me to work for your support ?" she asked. "It will not be easy for me to obtain pupils in the' country, without recommendation and totally un- known ?" Mrs. Narr smiled oddly. _

"You are not to trouble yourself, Dora," she said. " Your future is in our hands. Leave it all to us, your parents." Discussion and argument were alike vain. Dora became silent and thoughtful, but by no means resigned to her fate. The cab soon after entered the gates of the station, slowly ascended the rise, and drew up at the proper place. The Narrs alighted, with Dora between them, and hastened to the waiting-room. Here Mrs. Narr waited with Dora, while her husband pro- oeeded to the ticket office. He Boon returned, tickets in hand. "We 're in luck, 1" he exclaimed. "Train just going to start." He pulled Dora's arm within his and hurried her up to the train, Mrs. Narr following. A few minutes later the three were seated in a second-class compartment, in which were already a party of smokers, and were whirling swiftly over the arches toward the country.
CHAPTER XXV. THE BLACK COTTAGE-DANGER AHEAD.

Dora did not speak during the journey. The fumes of the tobacco choked her, and she opened a window and kept her face to the fresh night air, while her thoughts were busy with her pros- pects. The Narrs alighted at Chiswick, hurrying Dora between them to a cab, which they entered. "To the Black Cottage," commanded Jack Narr, pompously, as the cabman closed the door. "And let you' beast step oil lively." The driver mounted to his box, and the cab rattled down the street.

It was now nearly ten c'elock, an the long twilight had given place to the deeper shadows of the night. The moon was shining, and a myriad of stars were glowing, like angels' eyes peeping through the blue and fleecy crowds, and the warm, soft air was sweet with the breaths of flowers. Dora fancied she could distinguish the scents of the hawthorn and the dogros and with those odours came back to her the memory of Chessom Grange and the good old squire. After a few minutes' drive the cab turned into an unlighted street, or, more properly, a lane, where there were but few dwellings, and drew up before a high atone wall, in which a door was act.
"The Black Cottage, sir," the cabman an- nounced, descending and opening the door. Jack Narr gut out and looked at the place curi- ously..
Behind the high wall was a row of trees, which half concealed from his eager scrutiny a sombre looking dwelling, the sharp-pointed gables of which gave it a distinctive character.

"Yea, this is the place," said Narr. "I was down this morning to look at it. I have taken the cottage for a term. There was an old woman in charge this morning. She was to remain here till our arrival, but I don't see any light in the house. Perhaps she!s. cut and run with this young lady's
luggage, which Whti very valuable, and which I sent down this afternoon.

"You will be more likely to find out if you go into the house," suggested the cabman. "So I think," said Mrs. Narr, climbing out upon the ground, and compelling Dora to follow her. "You seem to want to tell all you know, Jack Narr. If yon 've got the key of the gate, why don't you fit it?" Thus catechised, Narr produced the key in ques- tion, and applied it to the gate lock. It fitted, turned, and the gate swung open. "We 're all right now," said Mrs. Narr, proceed- ing to pay the cabman. "Come along, Dora!" She seized the girl's arm and hurried her into the garden of the Black Cottage, and Warr closed the gate, which shut with a spring. The cab was heard going away. " At last," said Mrs. Narr, in an exulting tone, "we've got you entirely to ourselves. Dora. That young squire will never trace you here. There's a great gulf between your past life and this, and no one will be able to track you over it." The Narrs went slowly up the garden walk, their captive between them. The garden was a wide one, and walled in on every side. Upon the south wall peach trees were trained. Upon the other walls grape and rose vines clambered. In front of the dwelling was a lawn of limited extent, partly shadowed by the trees near the gate. The cottage itself, on nearer scrutiny, proved to be even more dreary and sombre than it had seemed at first glance. It was set low on the ground. Its colour was nearly if not quite black, and its funeral look was but slightoly relieved by the bright red colour of the window and door frames.

The cottage had been built by a bachelor of a glonmy turn of mind, and he had lived in it until his fleath, since which time it had been let fur- nished by the month to auy one who was able to pay, its moderate rental. _ _

the evening previous, after the discovery of Dora's flight from Lowater Crescent, Felix Warner and the Narrs had had a long colloquy, during which the former had advised the latter to procure lodgings in the country, and remove Dora thereto without delay. This counsel meeting with favour, Warner had sgmt out for a collection of daily papers, had looked over their advertisement columns, and had chosen from the long list of houses and lodgings to let the one offering the Black Cottage. He had then lent to Jack Narr a small sum of money, bidding him take the cottage at once. In obedience to this command, Narr had visited the place on the morning of the day on which he had captured Dora, and had taken it for a month. He had now come to take possession., "It's quite a grand place, Jack I" said MI s. Warr, with a gush of admiration. "Why, it's a 'gentleman's cottage! This is coming up in the 'world, I do sky !'

" 's nothing to what 's coming," returned Narr, swelling with importance. "We're going to live in such a house all the time, old woman. We 're going to have three hundred a year settled onto us for life. Think of that."
"We may be able to do better than that," said Mrs. Narr, tossing her head. "There 'a more 'n one path we can walk in, Jack." _ _

By- this time they had gained the steps and had mounted them. Narr sounded the knocker on the door. Presently an old woman admitted them, ushering them into a small lighted parlour. "Stay here with Dora, Jack," said Mrs. Narr, "while the woman shows me over the house before she goes." Narr assenting, his wife withdrew with her guide. Dora looked around her curiously. She saw at once that the cottage was of a grade greatly superior to any that the Narrs could have heretofore occupied. The engravings and books were beyond their comprehension. The furniture vias too quiet and simple for their tastes. "Who pays the rental of this cottage, Mr. Narr t" she asked abruptly. Narr was taken by surprise. He hesitated, and stammered out: "Mr. Warner!" Dora's face grew white with a sudden scorn. She began to comprehend matters. "Ah I" she said. "And why does he pay it ?" "Why—because he's took a fancy to us, Miss Dora, and wants to come and see us now and then. The truth is, he's in love with you, and the old woman thought you'd come round after a little—" He paused, half frightened by the sternness in Dora's eyes. "I see 1" said the you girl, gravely. "You have encouraged that man's vile propopals ?" Narr's looks answered for him.

"And yet you pretend to be my father r- "I -I couldn't help it, Mi,a Dora!" said the man, deprecatingly. "The old woman's to blame. The old woman's managed me all my life long, since I got into my scrape, and showed as how I couldn't take care of myself. Talk to her, Miss Dora. This Warner's well enough. He's a gentle- man—”

"A gentleman ?" interposed Dora, a world of scorn in her accents. "You mean he has money and influence—but he is no gentleman! I'd rather marry the poorest beggar in the streets than to marry Felix Warner. As to any other pro- posals he may make, he must never make them to me!'
At this juncture Mrs. Narr returned. She had dismissed the keeper of the house, and was in fine spirits.
"It's a beautiful place!" she exclaimed. "I mean to stay here by the year." "Perhaps Mr. Warner will buy it for us ?" sug- gested her husband.

Mrs. Narr cast a-quick glance at Dora. "Oh, she knows all I" cried Jack. "I told her that Mr. Warner paid all our expenses, and is com- ing to see us as soon as he can." Dora's cheeks flushed hotly. "He will never see me !" she exclaimed. "Don't be too certain !" replied Mrs. Narr, tauntingly. "I haven't quite made up my mind what I shall do with you yet. If you want to marry Mr. Weir, and if he'll outbid Mr. Warner, why, we may come to terms with him. And I've got another idea in my head, which I'll consider by and by. When I get ready to let you know, I'll tell you. Now I'll show you to your room." She took up a candle and led the way, Dora. and Narr following, They proceeded up stairs to a front chamber, into which the young girl was ushered.
The room wals fresh and inviting, with a bright Carpet and clan white curtains and bed draperies.

"Now don't try to escape or make us any trouble," said Mrs. Narr, setting down the can- dle. "If you should escape, you'd only be brought back. We are your parents, you know, and your natural guardians. And if you make US any trouble," she added, threateningly, "you'll suffer for it."

- • •••• Without waiting for a reply, she hurried out with her husband, and locked the door from the outside, withdrawing the key. "1 believe I hate that girl, Jack 1" said the Woman abruptly, as the; moved along the pas. Sage.

"Hate Miss Dora! Why 2" "Because she won't call me mother," replied the Woman, fiercely. "Because somehow I feel mean and small in her presence. Because she's young and beautiful, with high, proud ways, and you. and I are a drinking, lying lot. Why, she hates a lie, and she despises drunkenness; and—and she hates us."

"Well, hasn't she reason to ?" asked the more philosophic Jack. "She don't know anythhig about any reason," asserted Mrs. Narr, hotly. 'She'd ought to—to love us, when I tell her I'm her mother. I'd like to humble her proud spirit, and that's one reason I listened to Warner."
"I don't think the gal is proud," said Jack, dep- recatingly. "She's edioated, and all that, but she's gentle and soft-spoken, and too tender hearted to harm a worm."

" Bah ! I don't care what she is. I hate her. I don't believe in education and such fol-de-rols. If I'd known how things were going to turn out, that old Squire Chessom would never have got her. We sold her once to the squire' Jack, and I'm ready to sell her again to the highest bidder."
The woman spoke with a vindictiveness and malice that boded ill for the future of Dora.

"Come this way," added Mrs. Narr, fiercely, dragging her husband to the rear window of the hall. "Look out there. What do you see ?" Narr wonderingly looked out. He beheld the garden in the rear of the house, with a few trees and some neglected shrubbery. On this side, as on the others, there was a high stone wall, and beyond this wall was visible, in the. moonlight, a large and stately flower garden, which belonged to a handsome house fronting unother and wider street.

Jack speedily communicated his impressions. "And the house ?" asked Mrs. Narr, impatiently. "Do you see the house ?" "Of course I do. It 's all turrets and fixings, and must belong to nob._ What of it I"

Cut gu'eBs Who it belongs to " No," answered .Narr, stupidly. " How should I ?"

"'Well," said the woman, desperately, "it 'o ,ks almost as if we'd run our necks into a trap, That house, with the grounds adjoining ours, belongs to Sir Graham Gallagher." "Sir Graham Gallagher I" repeated Narr, me- chanically. "Yes, sir—that place belongs to Sir Graham Gallagher, the court physician," replied Mrs. Narr, excitedly. "The woman in charge here has just told me. He's been knighted since I Ilved in his family as his wife's maid. The House is calied Chiswick Lodge. And here we are, as you may say under his eye. He got me that child to nurse, and although he never had no suspicions of any- thing wrong, what would he think if he should recognise us? He would never believe Dora to be our daughter. He might suspect the truth." A cold perspiration bedewed Narr's forehead. "We'd ought to have changod our names more," he muttered. "I gave the name of Nancy—John Narley—to the house-agent and to the old womatli in charge. Wish I'd made it Wellington, or some such thing." " It's too late now," said Mrs. Narr, moodily. "We must keep out of Sir Graham's sight, and keep Dtha in the house. And we must hurry up matters, Jack. There's that old matter ot the forgery still liangiiiB. over us, and Sir Graham's presence here strikes inc like a blow. We must get Dora off our hands and make the best bargain we can for ourselves out of her."
"That's so !" ejaculated Narr. g‘ When will Mr. Warner be back ?.'
"As soon as he can leave Lord Champney, who is ill. Perhaps his lordsLip'll die. And if he does, I may make a trip up to Norfolk to see the Lady Barbara. '
Narr started, clutching her arm.
" You would not tell her—"

"I'm not a fool, Jack Narr. lam not going to send myself to a penal colony I All I want is to make ourselves rich. And Perhaps we can make the most out of Warner. But he'll have to raise his oilers if lie gets Dora. Leave me to manage the game. We hold the winning card. All we have to do is to keep a sharp look-out, avoid Sir Grat.a in, keep the girl close, and hurry up matters. Otherwise there's danger ahead !" (To be continued.)

MISS ANNIE OPPENIIETM, writing to Figaro eon- cermr,g the sort oY hair that denotes intellectual power, says :—" There is not any kind of hair that denotes intellect, the former being an animal matter." .Mist Oppcnheirn " firmly believes that b,-.ld-headed to,n ale the most that way inclined, they having througia the exertion of their brains exhausted all that is animal in their nature." AVOID extremes and "gush." Do not exaggerate the significance of trifles ; do not describe molehills as mountains. If a raindrop wets your face, do not say the storm was terrible; if a person is polite to Sion or does you a favour, do not immediately con- clude that he adores you and would die for you; if, on the other hand, he seems somewhat uneffusive, do not infer that he hates and would likt to kill you. Appreciate all good things, but do not senti- mentalise over them ; and do not "pour yourself out" when perhaps it might be just as well ao CO4l- - yourself. •

titiEsT or nolcorm.—an rmgnsn actor was a member of a company snow-bound in the Sierras while en route from California to the east. Before their train was pulled out of the drifts they had. been reduced to eating the coarse fare of the rail- road labourers, and got little enough even of that; so tlo.t they all had a magnificent hunger on when the train reached a small station at which there was a restaurant, and the Englishman was the first to find a seat at a table. "Bring me, in a hurry," he said to the landlord, a burly western man, "a porter-house •steak, some devilled kidneys, a brace of chops, plenty of vege- tables, and two bottles of Bass's bitter beer." The landlord stuck his head out of the dining-room door, and yelled to somebody in the rear apart- meat: "Say, Bill tell the band to play 'Rule Britannia.' The Prince of Wales has come."

ArrER they had kissed each other, the blonde said: "So Mamie is married?" "So I've heard," returned the brunette. "Nice girl," ventured the blonde. "Oh, very," returned the brunette. "I wouldn't say a word against her for the world." "Neither would I. How do you suppose she ever got him ? " "I am sure I don't know. Do you? "No. I would give anything to know." "So would I. It certainly wasn't her beauty." "Oh, no." "Or her cleverness." "The idea is absurd." "I can't understand it at all. They say she was married first by a justice, and afterwards by a minister." "I shouldn't wonder. She naturally wanted to make awfully sure of him." "Of course. It is the only way she could keep him; but I am glad she has caught some one. Mamie is a dear girl, and it would be cruel to say anything against her." "Indeed it would. I wouldn't do it for the world." "Neither would L"

It is perhaps rather early to introduce to our readers' notice anything in the bicycle line worthy their consideration, as the next season is rather distant,but the fact remains that you cannot know a good thing too soon. Even now many cyclists are casting around for a new machine and in get- ting one they will be advised well if they choose the Gormully and Jeffery tyre from amongst the host of others in the market. It is strong, resilient, speedy,and will stand a lot of rough riding. The popu- lar size is, of course, 1/ inch diameter,aud this tyre looks both substantial and neat on a wheel. Among the'special advantages of the tyre are the ease with which it can be detached, and the simplicity and safety of the valve. In the event of a puncture the outer cover can be removed from the rim in a mo- ment, without any straining of the fingers. After the inner tube is repaired, about 60 seconds is suffi- cient to fasten on the cover. The latter has a pro- jecting ridge round the edge (with no wire through it) and this tits closely into a corresponding under- cut groove in the rim of the wheel The tighter the, tyre is pumped and the more immovable it becomes. For serviceableness the " G and J''pneu- matic tyre is one of the best going. Messrs. Gor- ninny and Jeffery are American manufacturers, but they have an important depot in Coventry. Their avnts in Warrington are Messrs. Connah and Bel- lian, cycle agents, Bank Quay,

Of 'all the trade exhibitions which are now held annually in London, the Brewers' Exhibition is in many ways most remarkable. Phi year's show at the Agricultural Hall is fully equal to its predeces- sors. The brewers, maltsters, distillers, and their Customers who throng the show bear about them personally such unmistakeable signs of prosperity and content that they themselves form a comfort- able spectacle not to be equalled in any other gathering in this great world of London. The exhibits of/ machinery, materials, and processes reveal a confident enterprise- and ingenuity which the capitalists in few trades dare to practise in these days, and the exhibition irresistibly recalls Dr. Johnson's famous remark at the sale of Mr. Thrale's brewery, " Is is not a mere collection of tubs and vats,but the potentialities of growing rich beyond the dreams of avarice."

Considerable progress has been made with schemes of the War Office for the efficient protec- tion of London in case of invasion. These include the construction of forts on the top of Reigate Hill and Boxhill, as well as at Oxstead, overlooking the Caterham Valley. Several acres on the heights at Reigate and Boxhill were some time ago cleared of trees, and. the work has now advanced beyond this preliminary stage.

An official return gives the number of cases in Which a verdict of death from starvation has been returned during the present year by coroners' juries in London as seventy-one. This is double the number of the previous year, and although it is a shocking record, the number of officially certified eases is of course but an infinitesimal proportion of the real mortality in the metropolis due ever > year to laCk of the barest 'necessaries of life. In this great wilderness, where.so few geople, either rich or poor, know anything of even their next door neighbours, there is something peculiarly pathetic in the mass of acute distress side by side with a mass of active benevolence anxiously striving to give relief, and yet failing to come into contact until ins too late.

liGeneral Sir William Butler, in command of the South-Eastern District, has adroitly managed to squeeze one or two home-truths into his report on the recent manceuvres in Kent. He refers to "the bogey of the game ." as" that most potent influence Operating against the exercise of the Queen's troops over the Queen's realms." Even in getting a house for the beadquarter's staff ,opposition is always and frankly given by squires to the coming of Tommy Atkins—he might steal a bare I No doubt some in- cident of this sort occurring in Tory Kent gives point to the General's allusion. He makes another home thrust when he says that a body of troops moving over the country does the farmers less damage than is constantly caused by foxhounds.

The officials at the War; Office deny that there is any truth in the circumstantial statement tele- graphed from Cairo that the Sirdar of the Egyptian Army is on his way to England in order to confer with the authorities here as to an immediate ad- vance on Khartoum. They,however,admit that Sir IL Kitchener is on his way borne for a brief visit and the cpinion which he is known to hold about the desirability of attempting further conquest s in the Soudan makes it inequitable that his presence there will be a powerful influence tending to over- come the hesitation of the Government, if they are —as it is alleged—in a state of wavering uncer- tainty about future operations.

Prince Bismarck still continues to excite and amuse people here by his revelations'of the tortu- ous intricacies of German diplomacy when under his guidance, but those who commented • with cynical complacency upon the alleged double-deal- ing of Germany with Austria or Russia take a different tone in respect to the despatches from Berlin,which represent Great Britain,in her occupa- tion of Egypt and recent expedition into the Soudan as merely a cat's-paw of German policy.

It is stated that the Volunteer colonels who linger too long upon the stage are at last to be dealt with. The War Office are contemplating the exten- sion to the Volunteer forces of the rules of compul- sory retirement after a certain period, which are in operation in other branches of the service. Strong representations have been made by junior officers that the detriment to the Volunteer force by the block in promotion is not compensated by the( re- tention of the services of any commanding officer., however able, for a prolonged indefinite term of years. The whole question of improving the quality of the commissioned officers is affected adversely by the uncertainty with regard to promotion.

trader an energetic and vigorous secretary and executive committee the Eighty Club ha 9 entered on an extensive political propaganda for the winter all Over the villages and towns of England and in the Capital. On an average, ten meetings weekly are being held, and Yorkshire is coming in for a large share of the work. From the demands for speakers it is evident that there is a distinct awakening of Liberalism in the country. Last year the Eastern Question and education were the subjects most in request ; but this wititer there is a desire to hear political addresses on wider and more diverse topics such as old-age pensions,the land for the people,the House of Lords, political organisation, and how to preserve commons and rights of way. On the initia- tive of the women's organisations the Eighty Club is supplying speakers on the question of women being made eligible as county councillors A fea- ture in connection with the political work of the Club is the evidence of a spontaneous revival of interest in the Irish question. The financial rela- tions between England and Ireland will in this dir- ection form a chief topic of discussion. Arrange- ments covering the whole winter, and even up to April next, have already been made.

The resulte of the municipal elections have been closely examined in order to discover some indica- tion of the trend of political feeling in the country. It is, however, as a rule a futile endeavour, for political issues are too commonly over-shadowed by local and non-political considerations. I hear of one Qignificant Liberal victory which is also noteworthy because, by a clerical arror, it was tele- graphed all over the country as a Conservative gain, This was the case of the borough of Ipswich, which the Liberals fought on the purely political issue ,of approval or condemnation of the Rating Bill of last session. The result was an overwhelm- ing defeat of the Conservative leader in the Town Council, who has been a councillor for twenty-five years, and was looked upon as a future Tory mem- ber for the borough.

The second Commission on Old-Age Pensions held its first meeting for actual husinpss on Wednesday afternoon, and adjourned sine dielwithout doing' much business. This is the "fishing commission. which adopted the unnsual course of issuing a pub- lic invitation for all and sundry to send in schemes for providing old-age pensions. They have received many voluminous replies, most of which, however, appear at a first glance to bo hopelessly impractic- able, and the Commission is still a long way from providing the Government with a policy. In the agricultural districts the Tory promise of an old- age pension instead of the workhouse was the win- ming card at the general election, but now the la- bourers are saying in reference to the Rating Bill which the Government passed instead, "They pro- mised a pension to the labourer, but they've given it to the squire."

The excitement on the Stock Exchange on Wed- nesday afternoon due to the fluctuations in Ameri- can Securities was varied by one of those amusing incidents which occur from time to time when a too inquisitive stranger intrudes within the sacred pre- cincts. The luckless visitor on Wednesday found the whole place in an unusually boisterous good humour, and that section of it which is notinter- ested in American Securities with unusual leisure. The result was that he had a particularly warm reception. Amidst cries of "Kill him r "Kill him 1" • and shouts of laughter, he found himself hustled and jostled, and then carried shoulder nigh find flung out of doors. He fled up Threadneedle- street like a hare, pursued by some of the more athletic clerks, but at last secured the protection of a Policeman. '

div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
My DEAR NELLIE.

Velvet, felt, Chenille, and occasionally silk beaver, are the only wear just now as far as shapes are concerned; while for trimming, ostrich feathers are used in profusion, with satin, plain and miroir velvet, and wide ribbon. The newest ribbons are of glace or moire silk, with a narrow black edge of either velvet or satin, the velvet being prettiest and also most expensive, but it looks remarkably well and makes the most charm- ing neck ruffles also.

A pretty and fashionable hat is of red velvet and plumes of red and black feathers. This is one of the few hats which would be becoming to almost any style of face, and it can of course be repro- duced in any other colour. The quaint, short-waisted frocks, with • long, full skirts, are very becoming to slight children, and are altogether newer and more picturesque than those in Empire style, which are set in loosely from the yoke. Soft fabrics are essential to the set of these frocks, and if lined, the lining should also be soft and limp, or the graceful folds are lost,

For ordinary wear for a little girl, art serge is strong, cheap and effective, and the colourings are subdued and artistic. The front is slightly gored if a thick serge is used, otherwise three plain widths of 40-inch material are joined up straight, and tit, =.,ige hemmed over muslin, and three or five tu made above. The bodice is cut short- waisted and is joine.kl on to the skirt. At the top, the uncovered lining is filled in with gauzed or smocked material to form the chemisette or yoke. This should be made entire, and put on after the shoulders are joined up, and the bottom edge cut neatly away to slip in beneath the material. The braces and strap for yoke are of the material edged with very narrow coarse yellow guipure, and the cuffs are finished in the same style. The sleeves are closely shaped, and have a full pouff falling just above the elbow. A costume, a coat and skirt, is made of black tweed with a fine white line in it; a very popular stuff this, and an absolute simplicity marks its details for its own. The back of the coat is arranged like a gentleman's morning coat, with a centre lapped pleat and fiat pleats at the side seam. The front hangs loose and straight, and should ba arranged on canvas, and there should also be a strip of canvas on the left side to keep the ;mat firm and to support the buttons.

The rever q can }we enl irely of fur if desired, or of velwet, edgel uith tur, continuing the fur down the edge ot The This styl,3 of coat is also made with strapped and with plain lapels stitched at the e;iges. 'rue skirt, is plain except for two stitched tabs, f..l,tene,l with buttons, and meaoures four and a- ha I f yards round..

All the newest C,J41:4 re :very short, • and the frilly basque of la,t spring- has not quite disap- peared. There is, h,Twever, an exception to the rule of ehort coats allowed in the C ASO of the stout large won, whoni i short bascule would be most unbecom,ni; ; hi n,Ly Viear, if she likes, a coat fairly long in the skirt, ending about half-way between the hip and the knee. ,

Some charming evening blouses are.made of pale- coloured lawns and mudins, profusely trimmed with insertions and eilgir,gs of creamy Valen- ciennes lace. These dainty garments are very fresh-looking, and they are naturally much less expensive than silk 'bodice, which will no doubt commend them to the notice of young ladies who dress on an allowance.
Your loving JnIVNIE.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Although the Queen, from the very first gave her countenance to women riding tricycles, she decidedly looked askance for some considerable time at bicycle riding for our sex. Time however has worked a change in Her Majesty's opinions on the subject, and she now takes the greatest delight in watching the merry cycling patties which start daily from Balmoral. Comparisons between the entry into Paris of the young Empress of Russia, and that of our own Queen in 1885, have been much in favour in that city lately. It is recalled that when Her Majesty was obliAed by the rain to shelter under an umbrella, one of the crowd, perceiving that it was far too small and fragile to be of much use,offered his own which was graciously accepted. The next day he received his umbrella back, and with it a very beautiful gold snuff box Parisians are now finding out the truth of the old adage "After the feast comes the reckoning" for the cost of the Czar awl Czarina's five days' visit amounts to no less than £480,000 to £600,000. By the way, during the time he was travelling, the Emperor always had.his revolver, loaded in its six chambers, in a pocket of his carriage, just near his right hand. This revolver was given to him by his mother, the Dowager Empress, who extracted a promise that whenever he was away from the Royal Palace he would carry it with him. The wife of thenew Bishop of London has a command- ing figure at women's meetings, when church or philan- thropic subjects are under discussion. She is an im- pressive public speaker, has contributed largely to periodicals, and in 1882 Mrs. Creighton published a novel "The Bloom off the Peach." There is no doubt this book contains many passages of great interest and beauty, but is not strictly speaking, a clever novel, and had little success.

This year we have hardly had any autumn season, the summer came to an early close, soon after the end of August, and the prolonged rains have been followed by the premature opening of winter. This course of events has proved somewhat disastrous to those who laid them- selves out for a large business in autumn fashionthbut it has helped to lower the price of articles at the September and October sales, as numbers of women have been quite content, after carefully overhauling their ward- robes, to come to an economical determination to" make anything do this weather." The 'consequence will be that much intended for autumn wear, will be carefully stowed away and offered us in the spring, and that no very decided Change in the fashions will be forthcoming until the early summer cf 1897. There is no doubt that the formidable despite array of muffs to be seen in all our leading shops,thns particu- lar item of our toilette is less worn, except by middle- aged elderly women, year by year. For driving, the fur " grannies ' are, of course delightful, but for -Walking, thick gloves are much to be preferred, as they mean one encumberance the less to cope with in the difficultieet which inclement weather adds to our everyday life, when out of doors. A dozes years ago, a woman really needed five or six hands, if she was to manipulate her skirts, purse, parcels, and muff, but now we manage things better. Skirts are cut a sensible length for walk- ing, the purse is kept in a pocket, parcels are sent home by delivery carts,and thick gloves have dispossessed tpe muff.

The burglarly season has commenced, and wise f.c,ik will do well to remember to keep their houses just as safely barred and bolted in the upper regions during the early part of the evening, as in the lower during the nights, for it seems the favourite practice of the frater- nity who live by breaking into other people's houses to get in by a top u indow at dusk, and wait until the family and the servants are all safely in bed and asleep, before attempting to look round an help themselves, Speaking of burglars,thefts of milk left outside houses in the early hours of the morning have greatly increased of late, and householders will be glad to hear of an in- genious invention 'which is likely to cope with the nuisance in future. In a small ornamental plate, to be fixed on the door; there is a socket, and against this the milkman has only to press the can in order to cause it to become locked, so that no one can open the can till the door is opened. This little device will be welcomed by those of us who have had to go through the ordeal of drinking our tea or coffee without milk, because some individual, minus a conscience, has taken a fancy to our particular can I Before long bacteria are likely to be blamed for all the ills that flesh is heir to, for an authority on the subject now maintains that what we calf a "cold in the head" is really 'due to these invisible pests. " When," he says, "one enters a cold room after being heated, the bacteria in that room flock to the warm body, and enter by the open pores of the skin." Taking into considera- tion this disquieting item of news (only we are getting rather used to the idea of bacteria now) those of my readers who are not already aware of the fact, may be glad to learn that there are few things as efficacious for breaking up a cold as hot lemonade taken just before tedtime. It is best, to render this more effective, to bathe the feet of the patient in hot water and mustard before retiring, then give hot lemonade to drink. To make good lemonade,take a glass of hot water and into it squeeze the juice of one lemon, and sweeten to taste. This makes a strong lemonade and may not be fancied by some, but it is one of this kind that will do most good when used as medicine. For a ceugh,roasted or baked lemon is good. Put a good sized demon in the oven and let it remain until baked, which will be when the whole is quite soft,then take it out and add a quan- tity of sugar to make it a thick syrup. Take a tea-spoonful of this frequently, keeping it warm,and unless in a very obstinate case it will effect a. cure in a 'very short time.
" MADGE."

THE GILCHRIST LECTURES FOR WARRINGTON. •

The first meeting of the general Gilchrist Lecture Committee which was held in the Town Hall on Wednesday evening was a large and thoroughly re- presentative gathering, and certainly augurs well for the success of the lectures which are to be given in Warrington in January and February next. The Mayor (Alderman Fairclough) presided. and amongst the speakers were Mr. F. Monks, J.P., C.C., Councillor F. W. Monks, Councillor Roberts, J.P., Dr. White, J.P., Dr. Starkey Smith. J.P., Mr. Rymer Young, Mr. W. Long. Mr. Jeffery, Mr. T. Birchall, J.P., Mr. A J. Jolley, Rev. W. 11.Drum- mond,an4 the Rev. E.C. E. Carleton. Mr. F. Monks mentioned that the result of these lectures would be an encouragement or a discouragement to the Museum Committee in regard to following them up with lectures by first rate men on its own account. A resolution pledging the meeting to make every effort to promote the success of the lectures was passed unanimously.

div.head: roF friolLEsiy
div.p: roF friolLEsiy
A WARRINGTON PUBLICAN FINED.

On Monday morning at the Warrington Borough. Police Court before Mr. Monks (in the chair), Aldermen Francomb and Harrison, Councillor Pierpoint, and Messrs. Guest and Birchall, Henry Hughes, landlord of the Star and Garter beerhouse, Friars'-green, was charged with selling intoxicating liquors during prohi- bited hours on Sunday night, the 11th ult. and Owen Farrelly, 294 lin otsford-road, William Cosgrove, Wini- fred Cosgrove, 13 Arpley Walk, and Martin Mannion, Mill Lane, were charged with being on the premises at the time. Mr. Browne appeared for thp defence. The Chief Constable stated the facts of the case, from which it appeared that P.C. Cooper was on duty at 20 minutes to twelve on the night in question, in Friars'- green,when he noticed alight in the kitchen of the beer- house. A disarrangement of the blinds enabled him to see into the kitc'en to some extent. The man Cosgrove was in the middle of the floor dancing, and he said to the landlord and his wife "Let ns make a - big row, and no one will suspect us. They might if we don't." Cosgrove drank beer out of a glass, and a praysition was m ade for an adjournment to the taproom to have a "do." The officer, in anticipation of the "do," went for Sergeant Cheney and P.C. Clark, and all returned to the beerhouse, stationing themselves at different win- dows. The people were having supper, and all were having either beer or stout. The landlord proposed that another round should be brought in, and asked who was going to pay for it. No one seemed to answer,-but the wife gat up and went into the cellar and brought back a half gallon jug three parts full of bees, which she took into the taproom and put four glasses on the table. Mannion gave her 21 and other money, and Mrs. Hughes had a bottle of stout. Cheney then went to the front door and the officers entered the house. Some beer which had been freshly drawn was found in the kitchen. The landlord, when told that the matter would be reported, stated that he had asked some of hls customers to stay with him after ten o'clock and have supper with him. Corroborative eviderce was given by P.C. Frank Cooper, Sergeant Cheney, and P.C. Clark. In answer to Mr. Browne they affirmed that they distinctly saw the money paid. .

Mr: Browne: My clients deny having paid a half- penny. They are all respectable men. Mr. MAnks : It is a mark of respectability to pay your way. (Laughter.) Mr. Browne,for the defence, said that Flughes was shortly leaving the " Star and Garter." He had not been there long and did not knew that it was customary to send the Chief Constable word when a publican was having friends to supper. He was ignorant of having done wrong. He denied that any money was received or that the other defendants were asked for payment. They were all most intimate friends. Henry Hughes. the landlord. said Coagrove never danced in the kitchen. He did not know he was doing any harm in having a few friends there. Nobody said "Let's make a row etc." Defendant never received any money. He never saw any. Money was never mentioned.—This statement was borne out by the re- maining three defendai ts and Mrs. Hi•ighes. The Bench, after some minutes' consideration in pri• vats, said they had decided that the defendants most be fined ss. and costs each. The license would not be affected at all.

div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

1 There died in Cornwall a few days since a Mr. William Browning, whom his friends claimed to be the eldest Wesleyan local preacher in the world, not only because he had entered his 100th year at the time of his decease, but had been upon the " Plan " of the Launceston Wesleyan circuit ever since 1824. What is perhaps, of more general interest is that this venereble gentleman's father, who himself reached the patriarchal age of ninety- two, well remembered hearing John Wesley preach in a Cornish street. This is a link of recollection with the religious past which is more striking even than that of Mr. Gladstone, who can recall conversations with Arch- bishop Howley (who has had an successors in the Primacy Sumner, Longley, Tait, denson, and Temple), as well as with Sydney Smith. It was at the table of Flallam, the historian, and in 1833, that the famous canon of St• Paul's. talking to the future Prime Minister, discuised the improvement which was then becoming visible in the character and conduct of the clergy and remarked, "Whenever you meet a man of my age you may be sure he's a bad clergyman."

An interesting instance of" reciprocity "between the United States and England is (says the " Telegraph ") supplied by a letter which the American Ambassador recently addressed to the London School Board. It ap- pears that the New York Association of Sewing Schools is desirous of showing in the United States something of what is done for girls in English scholastic institutions, and the Ambassador was asked to obtain specimens of industrial drawing and designing, notebooks of scholars, , samples of sewing, with full explanations, showing the sequence of the lessons, together with any text books or reports which illustrate the working of the schools. Needless to say, the request has been granted without opposition and a committee authorised to prepare the samples, which will be displayed at an exhibition to be held in New York in January next.

There aro probably few people who have crossed the American continent entirely on foot. The feat, however, has been accomplished by Tobias Schuster,an Austrian, who seven years ago migrated to California. He .nvested his money in a farm which he cultivated w!th some success for a time. Two years ago, however,' his pro party was devastated by a swarm of locusts and a herd of wild pigs. In spite of his struggles,he was unable to pay the interest on the mortgage of the property,which was sold up. When the mortgagee was satisfied,Schrua- ter found himself the possessor of something less than half a sovereign. With this sum in his pocket and his portable property tied up in a handkerchief, he started to walk to New York, and has actually arrived there.

The Prince of Montenegro is no doubt glad enough to have got home again to his diminutive capital, for he seldom visits the busy haunts of men, and the restraints of royal life in a city like Rome were evidently irksome to him. As a matter of fact, during several days of his stay he donned the ordinary attire of a decent cittadino, and walked about the streets with his pretty young daughter, Princess Anna, quite unobserved. A little incident warned him to be more cautious. In one of his rambles he entered a tobacconist's shop to buy some cigarettes, and threw on the counter a golden twenty- lire piece in payment. Perhaps it was the clink of the metal on the marble that attracted the notice of other customers, to whom the sight of specie was a novelty ; but certain it is that they examined the stranger more closely, and one of them whispering, " Per Bacco 1 Nikita I" ran into the street before the Prirce could pick up the greasy bundle of notes that constituted his change. By the time he got on to the pavement a crowd had collected, and every instant increased its numbers. With his scared daughter on his arm the Montenegrin Sovereign had to take the shortest cut to the Quirinal, closely pressed by his impromptu escort.

The police recently made a search in a house at Liegnita, in Germany, and found in a bedroom a boy of ten who for two years had been constantly kept in a bed rolled up in furs and other warm garments, while all aocess of fresh air to the room was carefully pre- Vented. The unfortunate patient had been kept in this condition on the advice of a certain quack, who had, moreover, prevailed upon the boy's parents to give him over one iundred bottles of his nostrum. Taken to the hospital, according to the" Chemist an Druggist," the boy was medically examined and pronounced to be ab- solutely free from any organic disease.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Robert Plopley. Highfield Cottage, Canal Bank, was charged with causing a horse to be worked whilst in an unfit state on the 9th October. Frank Hopley, son, was charged with working the same. —P.C. Butler said, on the date named about 3 o'clock in the afternoon he saw the second defendant in charge of a horse and cart in Bridge-street. The horse was very lame, and appeared to be in great pain. Witness ordered the horse to be taken home. He saw the horse the next morning, and also on the 12th October, it was then in the same condi- tion. He drew the attention of the father to the heated condition of the animal's feet.—By Mr. 11. N. Linaker (who appeared for the defendants) : The horse was turned into a field in his presence. It was then lame. He told the defendant that he was not a veterinary sur- geon and could not tell him the cause of the lameness. Inspector Bilson, said he saw the horse on the 12th Oct. It was an aged norse, and was lame on the near hind limb. The cause of lameness was spasm. There was a considerable amount of pain and inflammation about the tendons. To work it on setts as described by the constable was certainly cruel —Asked as to how he came to work the animal in such a state, the defend- ant said it was not lame. The animal had been seen by Mr. Bate, veterinary surgeon of Sutton Weav r, and he told him not to work it on setts,but onfland.—ln answer to Mr. Linaker, Mr. Bison said he was not a veterinary surgeon, hut he had had 13 years' experience In veter- inary work, and also had to pass difficult examinations before he was appointed an inspector.—Mr. Bate, veter- inary surgeon, Sutton Weaver, said he saw the herse on 11th October. He gave hts opinion that the horse was not lame, and was fit to be worked. He had also seen the horse since and it was all right. It was not sufferiug from spasm.—By Inspector Bilson : He had been a wit- ness against the Society in many cases.—By Mr. Linaker: In every case he had appeared the Society lost the case.—lnspector Bilson : Did not the Society secure one heavy conviction in which you appeared P—Mr. Bate: No.—The magistrates after consultation decided to dismiss the case.

A machine for catching flies off the backs of cattle, and so affording the animals relief and comfort,has bf.en invented by an American farmer. The fly-catcher is a kind of covered nen or passageway, through whiph the animal must walk to secure relief. A few feet from the entrance there is a cupola or dome in the roof of the passageway, made of glass and arranged as a fly trap Beyond this the passage is darkness.. The animal walks thrnueh the machine, and just RR it passes under the dome and enters the darkened part a set of brushes sweeps off the flies, which naturally rise into the liehted dome, and the steer PARSPS out at the other side free of flies. The the; are retained in the through dome trap, The invenor has experimented with his m thanimals snn learniet valse nfatch2 fl h device.d ow enough to walk oaw the flies begin to bite.

div.head: COMMENCEMENT', OF THE SEASO
div.p: COMMENCEMENT', OF THE SEASO

On Saturday evening the second season of popular con- certs in the:Parr flail was commenced under most favour- able conditions. The building was filled in every part, which was a distinct proof that the public have by no means forgotten the excellent entertainments produced last season at such a moderate charge. The desolate appearance of the large platform was remedied by the tasteful arrangement of a quantity of plants from the Corporation greenhouses. Ar istes whose popularity was assured had been engaged, and nothing appeared want. ing to make the opening concert a success. The singers were Miss Ethel Hubi-Newcombe soprano, (Gold Medal- list, R.A.M. and winner of the Llewellyn Thomas Gald Medal,lB96), and Mr. Charles Aspinall,alto ; Miss Sophie Roberts (L.R.A.M.) was pianist ancl:acc.:;mpanist, while Mr. Mel B. Spurr was responsible for the humorous ele- ment. Miss Roberts was the first contributor to the even- ing's entertainment, and her tasteful interpretation of Raff's"Minuetto" was warmly applauded. Her ability as pianist was further evidenced when she, in the second part of the programme, vivaciously played " PaEci iidade " (Gotschalk). A rendition of " The Children's Home," by Mr. Aspinall, also met with appre- ciation. The singer's pure notes and clear enunciation were, however, displayed to perfection on his second appearance when " Saviour of all," a sacred song with words by Mr. Spurr and music by Bond Andrews, was submitted. Mr. Aspinall treated the solo cleverly, and its solemnity and fine effect were most pronounced, especially as Mr. Spurr played the organ obligato and Miss Roberts, the pianoforte accompaniment. A repeti- tion was demanded of the singer who complied with "Eileen Allannah," another song which well suited his voice. More than usual interest was attached to Miss Newcombe, owing to the fact that sloe belongs to the "good old town." Her first song was " I am Titania," (Ambroise Thomas), which trying piece of vocal music she brilliantly performed. No song could have been a greater test for Miss Nevrcombe's peculiar abilities and flexible voice,and she received a merited encore. In Testis "May Time," Miss Newcombe sang very sweetly but there was some difficulty in catching the words, which might have been obviated. Nevertheless another response was called for and the young artiste displayed her capabilities in ltalian,a language she seemed quite at home in. One other performer yet remains to be mentioned, viz. Mr. Mel B. Spurr, who is dealt with last from no reflection on his merits. On him was the greatest strain, for the programme contained his name in no less than four places.' His productions were " How we sing" (words by Spurr and music by Alfred R. Sutton)"What is a Gentleman" (zither accom- paniment). "The Liverwing Testimonial,"" Quick Work," and "Home for the Holidays." All these recitals, songs, and ',ketches were encored. Mr. Spurr was over- flowing with eccentricities, jokes, sarcasms, and fine humour. Ihe audience was in a state of perpetual mer- riment, and perhaps showed greatest appreciation of " Old Mother Hubbard" (recital), and "Home for the Holidays." Both were capital,and displayed Mr.Spurr's versatility to the best advantage.

div.head: DEATH OF LADY GREENALL
div.p: DEATH OF LADY GREENALL

At noon yesterday, Lady Greenall passed peace- fully away at Walton Hall, after a long and painful illness. On the receipt of the news at Warrington the flags at the Town Hall and the Liberal and Conservative Clubs were hoisted half-mast. Dr. White, of Warrinzton, has been her medical at- tendant, and Dr. Waters, of Liverpool, was also con- sulted, but despite all the medical skill brought into requisition, she died as stated. Tier husband, the late Sir Giloert Greenall, Bart., formerly the member for the borough, died on the 10th July, 1894, so that she has only survived him a little over two years. She was married to the late baronet in the year 1864 She was a daughter of the late Mr.Jetin Louis Rapp, and her family consists of the present Baronet,Sir Gilbert t-ireenall (who was born on the 20th March, 1867), and the Misses Susannah and Bertha Greenall. Since the death of her husband particularly, her ladyship has been a most liberal benefactor to local religious and charitable institutions, and her pecun- iary assistance in these and in other directions will be much missed. By her death, the Warrington infirmary has lost a warm supporter. Some time ago she generously presented the Corporation with the Mayoral chain. She had. for many years dis- played unbounded interest in the bazaars held in Warrington in aid of the various church organiza- tions, and had opened several in short but graceful speeches. Probably, however, it will be in the parishes of Higher and Lower Walton that tte greatest sorrow will be experienced, as she was always ready to ameliorate genuine cases of dis- tress. Lady Greenall was 65 years of age. The funeral will take place at Walton Church en Tues- day at 12 noon, and it is specially requested that no flowers be forwarded.

The funeral of the late Lady Greenall, of Walton Hall, took place on Tuesday, at Walter' Church. When a great number of people from Warrington were present to pay their last respects to the deceased lady, who has been most beneficent to the aged and distressed. The ccffin was met at the ball and placed on a bier. The procession from the ball included the late Lady Greenall's family and ene or two immediate friends. The coffin was followed to the church by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Miss Greenall, Miss B. Greenall, Mr. Cyril Greenall, Mr. Robert Davies. and Mr. John White. The procession proceeded down the main drive to the wicket gate opening on the church-yard, where it was met by numerous friends and tenants of tke !ate Lady Greenall, The officiating clergy were the Rev. L. J. T. Darwall, vicar of Walton, the Rev. Richard Greenall, and the Rev. H. T. Clark. The Rev. F. Slater, vicar of Sr. James'. Latchford, also took part in the service. The choir rendered the hymn " My God, my Father, whilst I stray," and tbe. Rev. R. Greenall read the lesson ap- propriate to the burial of the dead. Another hymn, " Brief life is here our portion,' • was also sung' after which the procession was reetormed, and proceeded to the graveside, the Dead March in "Saul "being played on the organ. The Rev. L. J. T. Darwall read the I service at the graveside, at which a numerous gathering was precut. The interior of the grave was lined with Iferns and moss, and a large wreath in the shape of a cross was on the coffin. Amongst those in the church were—Mr., and Mrs. Edward Greenall. Mr. and Mrs. Henry Greenall, Mr. Peter Stubs, the Rev. T. Whitley and Mr. J. Whitley, Mrs. Clark. the Rev. Il• V. and Mrs. Pigot, Mrs. Darwall, the Rev. E.C.E. Carleton and Mrs. Carleton, the Rev. A. A. Markham. the Rev. T. Gil- bertson, the Rev. B. Percival, Mr. Charles and Miss White, Mr. James Tinsier, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M. P., Mr. E. W. Woods, Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones, Mr. T. J. Down, Mr. J. R )binsen, and Mr. J. H. Clarks. The coffin was a very massive one, and was made of fumi- gated oak. The raised shield on the centre of the lid bore the following inscription :—" Susannah Gresnall, died 30th October, 1896, aged 65 years." The arrange- ments for the funeral were efficiently carried out by Mr. R. Johnson, of Bridge-street.

The second anmsai m-e-tting of the Warrington branch of the St. John Ambulance Brigade w held on Thurs- day evening in the Bank Clupy schoolroom. Mr. R. Morris, F.G.S., the Rev. B. B. PiTscott, and others. After an encouraging address by the chairman, the Secretary read the report of the committ7e and balance sheet for the past year. The report stated that a num- ber of classes have been Weld within the centre,includine Messrs. Crosfields' ',Works ; C.L.C. At the cl,.se of last year they had 69 names upon the register, 5 of these have left the district. and the 29 new members brines the total number of names upon the register up to 93. Efficient first aid has been rendered in 64 cases. The balance sheet showed that the receipts were £2B 194 3d. which included a balance from last year of £4 us. 81. ; the expenditure was £24 ss. 3p„ the balance in cash in the Treasurer's hands of £2 13, 110 i bringing the total to £26 19i. 31. A visit to "The Pantheon" will prove bsth instructive and remunerative. It is the Finest Furnishing Warehouse in Manchester, has an immense frontage of 110 feet, five storeys high, with a capacity of over 1,0.0,000 square feet of showroom, most brilliantl,, lit throughout with electrict light, has hits to all tbe floors, nJ contains ten times the stocu of furniture of any other house in Manchester. You can pay visit to" The Pantheon." walk through it with perfect com- fort and pleasure, see if there is anything you consider a bargain, entirely at your ease, and in perfect liberty,pleasing yourself whether you buy or not. If you wi-h to furnish a house for RIO or -25,000, WORSLEY'S can execute the order with marvellous rapidity, and you will effect a saving of quite 50 per cent. One visit to "The Pantheon," at Man- chester, will amply demonstrate the truth of these asser- tions.

div.head: CARPET DEPARTMENT.
div.p: CARPET DEPARTMENT.

This Department has had special and careful attention. All that experience and accurate knJwledge could acquire in all the markets of the world has been realised. Most carpet departments after a lapse of years develop a quantity of soiled stuck, which is very objectionable. The whole ot the stock at "THE PANTHEON."however,is spotlessly clean,perfectly new from the loom, the best rf patterns,the newest and most unique designs. The produet of the best manufacturers in Kidderminster and Yorkshire are now on show at "THE PANTHEON," Inclian,Turkish,and English Carpets in great variety, at keen, cutting prices. Immense quantities of Per- sian, Egyptian, Turkish, French.and English Itugs,and every form of Skin Rug. All carpets will be sold at old prices. We may indicate briefly the lines upon which this Department is worked by the tollowing prices,for,despite the recent advance in ca-pets, WORSLEY'S low prices for Ltanding qualities re- main the same :

Best 5 Frame Brussels, 3s 9d per yard. Special Ilrussis, 2s 9d par yard. British-made Axmiusters, 3s lid per yard. Ditto ditto, 5s 6d per yard. Ditto (Wool Bac!t), 5s lid per yard. Turkey Carpets,though dearer owing to the disturbances in the East. are offered at old prices. WOHSLEY'S being direct Importers of these Carpets are able to give exceptional value. Finest Deccan Hugs. 6ft by 3ft 9in, 12s 9d. Koula Rugs, Es 9d, lOs 9d, 153 9d, 21s 6d. Finest Mirzapore Hugs, 6ft by 31t. 21s. A magnificent sh w space has been allotted for the display of well seasoned Linoleums aud Oilcloths,all the newest pat- terns in colouring laid design, at prices from lOid to 3s 6d per yard.

div.head: CABINET DEPARTMENT.
div.p: CABINET DEPARTMENT.

This Department, which is the largedt, and forms the Chief Feature at WORSLEY'S, contains, without fear of con- tradiction, the largest. the most complete, and the most beautiful stock outside London. 30, Bedroom Suites from £3 17s. 6d. to £l5O are on show. 150 Dining-room Suites and 150 Drawing-room Suites, from £4 103. to 85gs., are also on show. " This will give you an idea of how varied and ex- tensive a stock of furniture it must be. Of course, accom- panying these chief features in the display there are all the thousands of articles which are necessary for furnishing. The grandest display of Bedsteads in the North of England, chiefly by those celebrated makers Messrs, Hoskin and Sewell, of Birmingham, are artistically shown, fitted complete with the usual accoutrements.
