We have gi;eu this brief list in order that our readers may form a faint idea of the immensity of the stock at WOES- LETS, and we should recommend all intending purchasers to pay a visit to THE PANTHEON"before deciding. The visit will certainly be interesting and instructive, and cannot fail to give satisfaction. "THE PANTHEON "is worth a visit, as it contains the finest exhibition of furniture to be seen out- side London. Everybody has perfect liberty to inspect the stock, which is all marked in plain figures, The prices are fixed prices, and will not be altered for anybody. All goods delivered carriage paid. Purchasers of any of the bedroom suites may have their money returned if not satisfied.
Our next advertisement Will contain a list of a purt'n of the Dining-room Suites, succeeded by one coat dning Aw- ing-room Auites and other miscellaneous furniture.
SECOND-HAND DEPARTMENT.

Mr. Worsley wishes to draw special attention to this de- partment, which forms one of the most attractive features of "THE PANTHEON." In this department there is every variety of furniture for Drawing-room, Dining-room, Bed- room. Library, and Office. The most astonishing bargains can be procured. Mr. Worsley has agents purchasing second- hand furniture from the leiding business centres of Great Britain, and the stoc,: thereby obtained will enable the work- ing man to procure a House of Furniture Complete for £2O, worth double the money. It will also enable the merchant to furnish with high-class, good old hand-made furniture by makers of great repute at prices which pulverise the com- petition of the new London furniture. Be Cautious not to Purchase New London Furniture. There cannot possibly be any satisfaction in purchasing the new jerry-veneeredorange- boxes, which the makers have the effrontery to call furniture, and which are knocked together in the East find of London. Second-haud furniture by good old makers having stood the test of time can be depended upon to give satisfaction. WOES- LEY'S have quite an army of cabinetmakers. French polishers, and upholsterers, whom they cliefiy employ in renovating the finest specimens of second-hand furniture, dn.!, if necessary, remodelling the same. They have an enor- mous stock of Antique Furniture, and exhibit the most in- teresting collection ever placed on show in this district. As a sample of the bargains that they can offer in this depart- ment they cite the case of a Sideboard by Doveston. Burre, and Hall cost £B5. Price, 18gs•

div.head: IN CONCLUSION,
div.p: IN CONCLUSION,

WORSLEY'S give notice that their terms of business will be cash, at the marked prices, but will have no objection to allow part of the purchase money to remain over,or to be paid by instalments, subject ti a charge of 10 per cent for the Convenience. This will sweep away the unequal and pernici- ous effects of the Hire System, which perhaps is responsible for more misery to young people than any system that was ever invented. The Hire bystem has .been denounced over and over again by Coinity Court Judges throughout the land as being little better than the money lending system. Pur- chasers have to pay through the eyes and nose for everything they have to get on the hire system, and then they arm liable to lose every penny they have paid, if they miss one of their monthly or weekly payments. WORSLEY'S will try to help the public in this matter, and instead of having to pay high prices they will sell them this goods at the plainly ixtarked cash prices, and charge then straightforwardly in a percentage upon the money unpaid. They have seen cases where chairs have been charged 7s. 6d. each on the hire system, which they sell at 3s. fel. WORSLEY'S will be delighted ii you call and inspect their stock, to prove the undeniable truth of their assertions.

THE great presidential election of The American Election. America is now a thing of the past,

and Mr. MeKteLey is to be the President of the United States, for the next four years. The contest has not been such a close one as was expected by the majority of impartial observers. The Republicans seem indeed to have carried everything before them. It had all along been taken for granted that while the more populous Eastern States would pall large majorities for MCKINLEY, the Western and Southern States would support the Democratic ticket. The result shows that the Republicans have held all that they were expected to hold,but that the Democrats have failed in several places where they were expected to be strongest. The "solid South" is now no longer solid in its sup- port of the Democratic party. There has, in fact, been a complete breaking up of American parties over this election, but the Democrats have been vastly more divided than the Republicans. This is a feature of the campaign which is regarded with anxiety by not a few of the more thoughtful Americans. It is reported that even now on the very morrow of their great victory the Republicans' or at least the most sober-minded amongst them, are not deposed to be excessively elated. .46. President is only elected for four years andthat is but a short period in the life of a nation. Ono leading politician on the winning side has declared , that the campaign for the next presidential terra has already begun, and there is reason to believe that this is only a striking and emphatic way of stating a real fact. Mr, BRYAN and the Democratic party have during the last few weeks brought new and almost revolutionary doctrines into the arena of Americao politics. Public opinion has not yet had time to shape itself in, regard to these new questions, but the shaping process will, we may be sure, be eon tinued during the next four years. div.p: Rryan, and consequently rapidly filled the Republican war-chest to overflowing. Bearing 511 mind all these circumstances the Demo- crats will probably maintain that though they have been beaten they have not been "wiped out." they have displayed something like a missionary fervour in their efforts to win over the electorate tO "free silver," and it is scarcely likely that their Enthusiasm will be utterly extinguished by the elections of this week. During the next four yeais they will be the attacking party and be in the Position to make party capital out of the inevit- able blunders of the party in poN% er. The Repub- licans have predicted halcyon days for the working- en of America in the event of Mr. MCKINLEY'S return. It will be utterly impossible for them to accomplish all that has been promised on their be- half, and every failure will be a weapon in the hands of the Democratic agitators. Four years hence the "swing of the pendulum," which, as we know in this country, is a great force in politics, tvill be in favour of the par'q which is defeated to-day instead of being against it, so that if Mr. tRYAN'S doctrines be only half as revolutionary aS they are said to be there is a lively time in front of the United States.
LIE report of the Select Coin- Food Adulterations. to ittee on Food Adulteration

raises some points which should be of general interest. Most people consume more or less milk and butter every. day, yet it seems that these two wholesome and nutritious articles of food often contain substances which rimy easily prove to be very deleterious. It is said that foreign butt& generally contains such pre- servatives as boracic and salicylic acids. These anV- Reptics answer their purpose very well so far as Preserving the butter is concerned, but it is a seri- ous question wheLher they are not injurious to at at least some of the people who consume the but- ter. Dr. Orro HunNua, a past president of the Society of Public Analysts, is. of opinion that these substances cause a disturbance of the digntive organs, and he says their use is prohibited in pearly all civilised countries besides our own. In the case of milk the use of injurious antiseptics is even more objec- tionable than in butter. Milk, as everyone knows, is pre-eminently the diet of young children and often of invalids, neither of whom are well able to withstand the evil influence of drugs. Mr. LLOYD, a chemist of the British Dairy Farmers' Association, mentions a case which an analyst had found thirty grains of boracic acid in a pint of rank, yet it is stated on the authority of another eminent scientific man that ten grains of borax daily would be dangerous to a child by retarding digestion, affecting the heart, andi causing erup- tions on the shin. The use of milk is recommended in certain ailments, but it is evident that the line should be drawn at drupzed milk. Yet the select ,Committee do not seem to take this view. They are evidently of opinion that the use of antiseptics is advantageous to the farmer and the milk-seller and that it should not be stopped. It is to be feared that no great benefits will be derived from the work of a Committee which is so lenient in its View of adulteration as this Committee appears to be.

div.head: PREStDENTIAL ELECTION.
div.p: THE PREStDENTIAL ELECTION.

SOME QUEER BETS. Writing on "Campaign Bets and Campaign Buttons" in the " Westminster Gazette," Miss E. L. Banks says : --" Betting in New York is not so exciting as in cam- paigns gone by. M'Binley men are willing to bet, but they find few Bryanites in their own State who are able to bet with them. But in the doubtful States, in the West and the South, money bets and other kinds of bets are being made, and will continue to be ?ado up to the morning of the election. The money bets not particularly interesting, but the other kinds of bets are, in really cases, extremely Original. In Liiinois two farmers, ona a Bryan man and the other a maßinley man, and sealed, anhave come to an aerangenient—signed d legally certified, too! which is to the effect that if Bryan is elected the Mainley man will have his head closely shaven and silvered over, while if M‘Kinley is elected the Bryan man will have his head shaven and gilded, the head to be kept in this state 'until the Presidential election four years hence. A Michigan girl and her fiancee, both WlCinleyites, have I agreed that if M,Sinley is elected their marriage shall take place the day following the election, while if Bryan is elected they will not get married at all, either to each Other or to anybody else. The idea is, I believe, that in the event of Bryan's election the young man's salary 'Will be so decreased and so insignificant that he would never be able to save up enough money to support a The girl's faith* however, in the triumph of Mr. M'ltinley must be very great, for she goes merrily on Preparing her trousseau and has sent out invitations for the wedding which reedlike any ordinary invitations, 'With the exception of a finely engraved postscript at the bottom to the effect that in the event of Mr. Bryan's elec- tion the wedding will be 'called off.'An Indiana Silverite IS to wear a straw hat for four years and go without an overcoat this winter if M'Binley wins the election, while if Bryan wins one of his neighbours will do the same. In this same State another man has promised to go to church every Sunday till a Democratic President is elected in ease Mr. Bryan fails to win the fight. The interesting feature of this bet is the fact that the other party to the affair is a Presbyterian clereymatewho is anxious to turn the Bryan man into a church-goer, and is so confident of Republican success at te polls that he has picked out a pew for his new-comer. If the State of Ohio goes tlemocratic,. an Ohio editor is to wear evening dress all day long in his office for six months; and if Nebraska, the horde of the boy orator' candidate, would be treacherous enough to go for Bryan's opponent, a pro- Minent young lawyer is tolbe hitched up to a dog-cart and driven through the streets by a Mainley neighbour. These ere only a few among the thousands of ridiculous Wagers that are being made all over the United States, and which ever way the contest turns, there are a good Many A merican men, and women too, who, to say the least, are bound to have some original experiences 'Within't he next mentb."

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.
! EARLESTOWN v. LIAYDOCK.

The r!eturn friendly fixture between these clubs was brough t to an issue on the Earlestown ground on Satur- tay afernoon, resulting in a draw of one goal each. Earlestdiwn placed three new forwards on the field the Dick of these being Morris, who played all through, cor- rect football. Clarke took Wilkinson's place at full back,anid Aldridge played vice Taylor, Stevens filling the gap cat,..sed by Ramsey's non-appearance. There was a Lair attemdance of spectators, Haydock kicking off down hill. They at once visited the Earlestown goal, but Clarke ,and Mather repulsed, and an incursion was made into the Haydock territory, a corner having to be con- Ceded.Tlehe ball was got away,and play for a time hovered about m id-field. Haydock finally broke away and some clever pa ssing landed them in front of the home goal,but Casey saved. Each goal was alternately visited, but balf-time rrived with a clean sheet. On crossing. over Xiaydock got an opening, and breaking through all op- Dosition Ca sey was beaten. This reverse put some spirit into the garne,and getting away after the kick-off 'Tucker pas. ied to McEvoy, thence to Morris, who shot Over to the right wing,and Harrison equalised for Earles- town within two minutes. The game afterwards be- came of a rough character, for which Haydock was re- -BPonsibls,and several of the players were winded. Earles- town however messed considerably, and bombarded the Elaydock goal,bLkit were unable to obtain a lead, and the Rune ended as sated above. To-day their match with Bamfurlong, Earrestown will play a new goal keeper, Pollitt late of Wes t Manchester,in place of Casey, who is retiring.

IHE RIGBY CHARITY, RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Parish Church on Saturday afternoon the distribution of this charity took place. A short service was conducted by the Revs. W. H. Stables,H. B. Firth,and W. Scholes, after which 53 articles of under- clothing were distributed amongst the deserving resi- dents in the parishes of Runcorn, Halton and Weston.

div.head: -THE NEW RIINCOIZN THEATRE.
div.p: -THE NEW RIINCOIZN THEATRE.

The foundations for this place of amusement are now being laid. The building is to be of brick with stone dressings, and will measure 50ft. by 97ft. The conveni- ence of both artistes and audience will be altogether improved. The ventilation is to be on the modern prin- ciple, and there will be every provision for extinguishing an outbreak of fire. Special exits are to be erected and used in case of panic. Mr. Wiliam Farrell is the con- tractor, and Mr. S. Davies the architect.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO M. JAMES LITTLER.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO M. JAMES LITTLER.

On Monday a meeting of the congregation of the Parish Church, Runcorn was held in the National schools for the purpose of presenting to Mr. James Littler an address and a valuable solid silver tea and coffee service. The Vicar (Canon Maitland Wood) who performed the ceremony, referred in touching terms to the splendid work done by Mr. Littler, as conductor of the Parish Church choir. Mr. Littler suitably responded, and re- ferred to his connection with the choir. There was a large attendance. THE RUNCORN TRADEs' COMNUTTEE,_

A meeting of this committee was held on Monday at the Town Hall. Mr. P. Speakman occupied the chair, and at a later period, Mr. Jones presided. The report submitted by the sub-committee,showed that everything had been done in the way of trying to attract and in- duce new industries to the town. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi was appointed a member of the sub-committee which was re-appointed. DEDICATION FESTIVAL AT THE PARISH CHURCH, RUNCORN. The festival of this church was celebrated on Sunday. In the morning, owing to the unavoidable absence of the Rector of Warrington, the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. W. H. Stables. In the evening to a crowded congregation, the Vicar preached, and spoke of the fes- tival they were celebrating. The choir rendered special musical services both morning and evening, and on the latter occasion they sang the chorus from " The Messiah," " Worthy is the Lamb," wit') great precision. They were under the conductorship of Mr. James Littler, who for the last time officiated ia the capacity of hon. choirmastsr, consequent on his removal from the town.

div.head: ROBBERY AT A RUNCORN WATCH-SHOP,
div.p: THE ROBBERY AT A RUNCORN WATCH-SHOP,

On -Saturday morning,—at liuriCOrn Police Court, before Mr. F. J. Norman, a sailor named Samuel St. Clair was charged on remand with stealing a purse containing £3 13s, 6d. from a drawer in the shop of George Moores, Regent-street, at four o'clock on the afternoon of the 13th October.—Mrs. Moores repeated her evidence as to the prisoner purchasing a metal albert, value 6d., for which he tendered 2s. 6d. She toA th., change from a purse in the drawer, after which he left, and she went into the kitchen. In consequence of what Mary Ellen Santley told her, she subsequently went to the drawer, and found the purse and contents had been taken.— Mary Ellen Santley,of Granville-street,stated that on the day in question she saw the prisoner come from behind the counter in Mr. Moores' shop, and run away.—ln or- der to complete inquiries the prisoner was remanded for another week.
SIR JOHN BRUNNER, M.P., &ND THE EDUCLTION QUESTION. _

On Saturday afternoon, the corner stones of a new Unitarian school were laid at Heywood by Mr. R. D. Holt, of Liverpool:and Mrs. William Henley, of Hey- wood. Sir John Brunner, M.P., should have laid one of the stones, but as he was prevented from attending. Mr. Holt took his place, In his letter Sir John Brunner wrote that he had been hoping against hope to be able to at- tend, but he dare not. Though his usual health was re- stored, his voice had not ;et returned, and he would have been inaudible except to a few. The letter con- tinued :—" If I had been privileged to address tha gathering of your friends to-morrow, I should have en- deavoured to show that the claim of a powerful party to purchase from the State, by voluntary subscriptions, the right to force upon an unwilling community the teaching of formularies distinctive of a sect is a claim directly in opposition to the injunction " Do unto others as you would they should do unto you." I should also have had a word to say about the contrast between the terms in which the Church doctrines of to-day are des- cribed in Congress and what I may call the pre-Dar- winian methods of religious teaching in the ordinary national school. If sve could but have on all hands a de- sire for fair play and a love of sincerity, we should soon have both peace and progress." RUNCORN CARETS OF TEMPERANCE (GUIDE OF YOUTH SECTION). _ _

A very interesting meeting of the above society was held on Saturday evening in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom,under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Whyte, when two handsome books, which had been given by Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, were presented to the two boys who had got the largcst number to join during the pre- vious six months. Mr. James Johnson, the secretary, gave the report. The society is in a flourishing financitl position,having a large surplus to its credit at the Bank. There are now on the beoks 90 members, 14 having joined during the past half-year. The first prize was won by Master Frank Johnson," Real Grit," by Silas K.Hocking ; and the second was given to Master Wilfrid Whyte," ThBse Boys," by L. T. Meade. Mr. Edward Key in making the presentation, congratulated them on their succees in gaining so many members. It was without doubt one of the best societies for the young. He dwelt on the evils of drunkenness, especially among women, and he strongly advised them never to touch drink on any account, SiO that they might grow up sober men. Mr. Thomas J. Holt also gave an ad- dress, in which he spoke of the prevalence of drinking among both men and women. He also referred to the craving for drink among the victims of intemperance. He mentioned the causes that had induced him early in life to identify himself with the temperance movement. Messrs. James Johnson and Thomas Whyte moved and seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Bisbrown for the gift of books,and it was announced that Mr. Thomas Heesotn had promised to give two prizes in the next half-year. A pleasant meeting was then brought to a close. SCENE IN THE WESTON WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

Whilst attending divine service at the Weston Wes- leyan chapel, on Sunday eveningt Thomas Peoples, resid- ing with hie parents in Weston-road, Weston, was suddenly taken ill just at the conclusion of the service and when the congregation were leaving the sacred building, he fell from his seat on to the Boor as if in a fit. Assistance was at once rendered, and the patient was removed to a neighbour's house. He was afterwards conveyed home and medical assistance at once summoned. Peoples was bitten by a dog belonging to his parents some time ago, and from the symptoms displayed it was feared that the young man had an attack of the awful malady, hydrophobia. Several local medical gentlemen have been in constant attendance. During the convulsive seizure the patient was most vio- lent, and had to be forcibly held down. The decision of the medical men, is that the case is not one of hydro- phobia, but one that is very similar,and which is known as" false or pseudo" hydrophobia. The fast that the young man had been bitten by a dog, somewhat aggra- vated the symptoms. His condition last night (Thurs- day) was much improved. THE MARINERS' CHURCH, RUNCORN. - -

"My summer trip to Canada." was the title of a lecture delivered by the Rev. D. E. M:Si:nmonds in the Mariners' Cnurch, Irwell-lane, Runcorn, on Wednesday night. The lecture was illustrated by lantern views of Canada. The proceeds were in aid of the Colonial and Continental Church Society. There was a large audience.
GUNPOWDER PLOT.

The anniversary of this plot was celebrated at Run- corn last night. About 5 o'clock fires were to ba seen burning away in the fields and on waste land. Fire- works were going off up to a late hour. There were one or two minor accidents, but none of any serious nature. BILLIARD HANDICAP.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO • RUNCORN RAILWAY SERVANT.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO • RUNCORN RAILWAY SERVANT.

A presentation of a very. pleasing character was made on Tuesday,in the waiting-room of the Runcorn Station to Collector Collings,who is leaving the district for South Africa. Mr. Newton, clerk-in-charge, spoke in terms of praise of their c-worker. Mr. Collings suitably re- sponded. Messrs. Howard. Hughes, Yarwood, Wooley, and Walls, also spoke of their long association and ploasant experiencds with Mr. Collings. SAD SCALING FATALITES AT RUNCORN. -

Last night two young children died from scalds at Runcorn on the 18th October. Margaret Ann Dodd, aged three years, daughter of John Dodd, By- rom-street, upset the teapot which was on the table, and received-severe scalds about the face,neck,and chest. Despite the attentions of Dr. Ormsby she died last night (Thursday). In the second case Raymond Firkin, aged one year and eight months, son of Joseph Firkin, boat- rnan, Ellesmere-street, died under similar circumstances. The little fellow upset a jug of cocoa on him, whillt his mother was in the shop. Dr. McKenzie was in attend- ance, but the child died about 7 o'clozk last night.

The latest returns received from New York at the time of writing give Mr. M`Kiolev 277 votes and Mr. Bryan 170 votes in the Electoral College. A correspondent at New York says it is already settled that the Will will be cabled by the Ilepublicau Goverment.

r E EXAMINER SAVURPAY NOVFIVIBER 7 1896 r.vify,o,o/or ,qclloor, BOARD. $., The monthly meeting of tfit3 Runccrn School Board was held on Tuesday evening in the Board Room, town Hall. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were also present, the Rev. Canon Wood, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., E. Imison, C.C., F. J. Norman, J.P., E. Timmins, and G. Moss (clerk). SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. This committee recommended that proceedings be taken against twelve parents for sending their children irregularly to school. The visitors reported that the number on the rolls was 3,452, being 32 less than in the c3rresponding month of last year. The average attend- ance was 2,938 showing an increase of 57 ot the same period. The percentage of attendance was 85.1 which was considered very pod.—Mr. Imi3ou moved the adoption of the above minutas.—Mr. Norman seconded and they were carried. SCHOOL SAVINGS BANE. The Clerk presented his report for the year ending August 28th, 1896, and stated that it was satisfactory to find these institutions were thriving in spite of bad trade and want of employment. The total amount de- posited was £169 Os, 7d., being £24 more than last year. The repayments were £l6O 14s. 11d., being £33 more than last year. The balance to credit of depositors was £93 193. id. being £lO more than last year. The num- ber a accounts open was 236 showing an increase of 19.
TRU PROPOSED SECONDARY EDUCATION

The committee appointed to confer with the Technical Instruction Committee on the subject of introducing secondary education into the town reported that the committees had met,but after a lengthy discussion came to the conclusion that they could do nothing in the matter at present.—Mr. Imison said they could not make use of the Technical Institute because of the re- quirements of the Education Department involving structural alterations, which they would not be able to make. Is regards Mr. Marshall's scheme, he would not like to say that the scheme was practical, but certainly it was the only one before them. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi acted as spokesman for the Board, and he suggested that a professor be engaged to teach Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. (Laughter.) There was no demand at present for higher education. The committees thought they should like to have some more information on the subject before they decided. It re- quired a very great amount of consideration.—The Chairman said he regretted that he was not able to at- tend the conference. He should be glad if the conitnit- tee could find a practical solution. Although no scheme had yet been approved, he hoped one would be before long. The question of higher education had pressed it- self upon the country, and'also upon their town. Ho thought they had no greater demonstration than the knowledge they had in regard to their evening schools. They were in the seventh season for the boys and the fifth for the girls, and every winter they found that there was an increase at these evening classes. The only thing the Board could do was to establish a higher grade school. If they had to undertake it another building would be necessary. If it could be established in conjunction with the Technical Committee then it 'vould be better. But for the present he proposed to crl7op the subject,but he hoped the Technical Instruction (..)mmittee had the matter in hand,and that they would soon see their way to carry the scheme of secondary education into immediate action. This concluded the business.
A NORWEGIAN SAILOR DROWNED AT RUNCORN.

Oa Sanday night, a Norwegian sailor, named Ola Hulsen, aged 21 years, a native of Rica, and an ordinary seaman on the barque Josva,was drowned in the Weston portion of the Bridgewater Canal. The deceased, whose vessel only arrived at the Runcorn lay-by on Sunday afternoon, went into town with five other sailors about six o'cluck in the evening. They visited different pub- lic-houses, where they had drink. At 10.30 Hulsen, accompanied by Oscar Christonsen, belonging to the Bishop Burr, started for their vessels, which were lying side-by-side in the Ship Canal. After passing the china clay warehouses, arm-in-arm, deceased slipped and fell into the water. His companion tried to reach him, but failed, after which he ran and secured a iifebuoy. which he threw to him, without success. On reaching his ves- sel Christonsen told those on board what had happened.— Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest on the body, at the Cemetery office, Runco:n on Tuesday afternoon. After a good deal of evidence had been taken, Inspec- tor Hicks ssid he had sc3n four captains at the lay-by that morning. They drew his attention to the life-buoys which were fastened to the wall. They considered that there was no facility for foreign sailors, who were in the port, for saving life. They suggested that there should be lines and life-buoys in these dangerous places. Red lamps with the lines and life-buoys close to would be very handy. By the red lights they would be able to tell *here these life-saving articles were. He (the in- spector) thought it was a very good suggestion if the Ship Canal Company would carry it out.—The Coroner addressing the jury said his attention had been called to the fact by four independent captains, belong- ing to vessels who traded with this port, that there should be one or more life buoys, and lines placed in these dangerous parts for the safety of sailors who fre- quented the docks. There should be a lamp or lamps with red glass the lines and buoys beingt fitted close to so as to be easily detached. He could not exactly say from memory how many inquests he had held on people falling into the canal. He could say at least about 30. The foreman of the jury, with any other of the jury and Inspector Hicks should meet the Ship Canal Company, with a view of having the suggestion of the captains carried out. His experience was that if the Ship Canal Company saw that such a recommendation was bene- ficial. they would carry it out.— The jury returned a verdict of" Accidentally drnwned."

WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS, RUNCORN B RANC EL The annual sermons in connection with St. Paul's Branch of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society,were preached on Sunday in st. Paul's Church, before large congregations, by the Rey. F. %V. Macdonald, one of the joint secretaries, London. The annual meeting was held on Monday evening in the chapel. Mr. F. J. Norman, J.P., presided, and he was supported by the Revs. F. W. Macdonald, A. W. Hall (late missionary on the west coast of Africa), T. Brackenbury, W. George, R. J. Clifton, and J. Stafford, •rs. J. Simpson, T. Simister, P. Speakman, J.P., C. Aid., A. R Norman, S. Taylor, J.P. C.C., R. H. Poe- nett, E. Taylor, J. Unsworth, G. Bellamy, R. Rawlinson, and J. Lea. The meeting was opened with prayer. The Rev. W. George read a summary of the general report of the society. He pointed out that they had 363 missionaries and assistanta on the foreign field. They had charge of 42,637 full and accredited church mem- bers, and 9,410 on teal, mad 84.113 children in the day and Sunday schools. The income for the year was £123,757 7s. whilst the expenditure had been £124,720 9s. 51. On the year': working there was a deficiency of £963 83, 10d. The previous year the deficiency was £30,478 15s. 10d., but up to last Christmas there had been received towards that debt £26,655 153. 3d. The Liverpool district contributed £7,196 153. 7d. of which the Runcorn circuit forwarded £276 is. 7d. (Ap- plarse.) Mr. E. Taylor read the lccal report. He explained that the average sum cont i buted per member through- out the connection was 4s. 7d., that from the Liverpool district 6s. 7d., and last year that from the Runcorn circuit 7s. 9d. There would be no deficiency if every circuit came up to theirs. The amount collected in connection with Bt. Paul's congregation and schools was £36. Brunswick school, the boys contributed £l3 3s. 55., and the girls £6 is. 81d. By books the boys realised £l6 Os. Rid., and the girls £42 17s. 7d. The collections taken the previous day amounted to £l2 7s. 6d., making altogether a total of £139 83. 9d. 4The Chairman in a few remarks said they were there not to defend missions, or avologise for them, they were motto support and extend them. Their fathers had con- ceived the magnificent project of carrying to the dark places of the earth the boundless blessings of ci rilisation and they, their sons,were pledged to carry on the work. (APplause.) The Rev. A. W. Hall gave a very interesting address on his missionary work and travels on the gold coast. f IThe Rev. F. W. MacDonald also spoke of the good work performed by the :nissionaries abro id. The usual vote of thanks to the deputation and Chairman closed the proceedings.

The quarterly session of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Template was held on Monday night at the Co-operative Hall when there was a very good attendance. Bro. W. Wilson, C.T. prerided. Arrangements were made for holding a public en- tertainment next Saturday evening. The usual re- ports for the past quarter were suomitted. Bro. R. W. Nicholson reported an active quarter's work,the District lodge session having been held at Hades- tewn, and the anniversary of the lodge celebrated. Two visits had been made to other lodges. The membership was 109 in good standing, being a slight decrease on the prrivious quarter. Bro. J.I Sharrock, financial secretary, read the financial re- i port, showing a good balance in hand after meeting all liabilities. Bro. Newman gave an interesting report on the juvenile temple showing an improve- ment both in members and finances. The officers for the ensuing quarter were elected and after- wards installed by Bro. J. Taylor. C.C.T., as follows: Brother W. Wilson, C.T. Sister A. Jackson, V.T., R. W. Nicholson, secretary, J. Sharrock, financial secretary, J. T. Holliday, treasurer; S. Parker,chap- lain ;W. Reynolds, M.; G. Clarke. P.C.T ; T. Frith, guard, E. Newman, (sentinel) ; pianist,W.Willis. The usual committees, sick and , absentee visitors, and finance, were appointed.
IMPORTANT ACTION AGAINK SHIP CANAL COMPANY

ALLEGED EXCESSIVE ABSTRACTION 0: , AT WARRINGTON. In the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice Mr. Justice Kekewich on Wednesday, in the action af Fairclough and Sons v. The Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany,heard a motion for sequestration on behalf of the plaintiffs,the Company not having obeyed an injunction granted against them by his Lordship in November, 1894, limiting the quantity of water they should ab- stract, for their canal purposes,from the stream running past and supplying plaintiffs' Mersey Mills and How ley Quay. Mr. Warmington, Q.C., with him Mr. T. R.' Hughes, was counsel for the plaintiffs ; and the defend- ants were represented by Mr. Fletcher Moulton, Q.C., with him Mr. Gripes. Q.C., and Mr. Leigh Clare. In stating the plaintiffs' case, Mr. Warmington said it arose out of a breach of injunction granted by his Lord- ship, on the Ist of November, 1894. His Lordship asked did not the case go to the Court of Appeal, and counsel replied that his Lordship gave the plaintiffs judgment, which by arrangement was trans- lated :into an order. The order coming before th'e Court of Appeal, they did not entertain the question of construction of the Act which his Lordship had adopted, and on which the present proceedings turned. The facts of the case were these :—Prior to the Act under which the Ship Canal was made the whole of the river Irwell contributing to the Mersey, and the river Mersey,flo wed down, except a small cut which ran into the Bridgewater Canal, past Howley Quay and the Mersey Mills, which were occupied by the plaintiffs. The flow at Howley Quay and the Mersey Mills was proved in ordinary dry weather to have been between 90 and 100 millions of cubic feet every 24 nours, the minimum in dry weather being 74 millions—the lowest record, he be- lieved ever known. The Mersey Mills of the plaintiffs were worked by water power. Under the Ship Canal Act the Company were empowered to impound water in the Mersey and Irwell, and to appropriate such portions of the river as might be rendered unnecessary by the construction of the canal works—which powers had been exercised in some degree. But by the 88th clause of the Act it was provided, " for the protection of Warrington and its traders, manufacturers, and others carrying on business at or near that place,"that the Company should not within any 24 hours abstract or divert from the Mersey or allow to flew therefrom into the canal such a quantity of water as would diminish the downflow of the river past Howley Quay to below the quantity set forth in a schedule to the Act. What had happened was that the plaintiffs had suffered considerably from the Company's abstraction of water not being kept within these limits. The result was the plaintiffs' earlier appli- cation to his Lordship, and the interim injunction which he gave them, in effect holding that what the defend- ants had done was in breach of the Act. This was car- ried to the Court of Appeal, who made no order upon it, but upon the question of construction of the section the parties drew up, by consent, an order restraining the abstraction complained of, the injunction being sus- pended for a twelvemonth for the construction of works necessary to enable the Company to comply with the order. His Lordship asked did not that concede the construc- tion he had put on the Act. Mr. Warmington said he submitted it was so. The defendant Company had constructed tilting sluices at Woolstnn Weir, and he proposed to tender evidence on what had resulted both there and at Latchford Lock. By shutting down the sluices at the weir and lock they were able to create, and did create, a pond or pound bf water for a distance of about ten miles above Latchford, and so to prevent any flow of water at all. The plain- tiffs from this had suffered pretty well continuously,but their evidence was particularly directed to the months of May and June, 1898. That May was a dry month, but it was in dry weather the plaintiffs most felt the absence of low. They had the affidavits of Mr. C. H. Beloe, a civil engineer living at Liverpool, that from the 7th to the 30th ofjMay the average flow was 351 million to 391 million cubic feet; but although Mr. Longdin surveyor to the Warrington Corporation, differed Longdin, these figures, the result was practically the same, because his tests covered from the Ist to the 31st of May, whilst Mr. Beloe's were from the 7th to the 30th of that month.l In June things were worse. On theist, from 35 to 35i1 million cubic feet passed Howley Quay; on the 2nd, 14f million was the computation ~f one and 15i the I other. The result was that the plaintiff's mill was' stopped for 131 hours, such a thing never having hap- pened before the canal was opened. On the 3rd of June the measurements were 20i million by one and 211 the I other, and the mill was stopped for nine hours. On the 4th of June the measurements were 30 million and 271, and the mill had to be stopped at various times. Of course this was an extremely important matter, as it spelt ruin to the mill as a water mill. What made it all the woree was t hat the plaintiffs had neither control over the matter nor did they receive any notice when the sluices were to be shut, but Yore entirely, at the mercy of the Canal Company. The only substan- tial answer of the !defendant Company to the plaintiffs' complaint was embraced in the affidavit of Mr. Hunter. their engineer, to the effect that there had been no breach of the injunction,anci giving figures as to the flow of water. In opposition to this counsel put in the affi- davit of one of the partners in the plaintiff Company during the last 21 years, to the effect that the Mersey mills did not suffer from a deficiency of water for driv- ing purposes before 1893, but since then they had frequently been stooped for want of water, and they had also on many eccasions had to work under less than full pressure. Details of measurement of the water were appended to this affidavit, and also to one put in from Mr. Beloe : and, in conclueion, Mr. Warmington sub- mitted that the plaintiffs were entitled to the relief they asked. For the Canal Company Mr. Moulton reminded his Lordship that there was no allegation in the case that they had broken the injunction, but his Lordship re- marked that if this were so, the parties being there, he did not think a technical objection of that kind should 'be taken an what was perfectly understood was the case to be raised and fought. Mr. Moulton then pointed out that the injunction was not that the Company were to guarantee, but that they must not abstract, and they were, he said, prepared to do that to the full. They said they could only take 10 million cubic feet, and they did not take so much. , His Lordship : That is the question to be tried. Mr. Moulton said he proposed to cross-examine Mr. Longdin on his affidavit, but before doing so, if the Court was asked seriously to consider a suggestion in one of the affidavits filed in the case, that consequent on a supposed underground leak, some 20 million feet es- ' caped each day,he desired to be allowed to call witnesses on the point. His Lordship said that request might be considered when the time arrived, should it be reached, and mean- time Mr.Longdin's cross-examination might be heard. Mr. Longdin accordingly entered the box and,at some length was questioned by Mr. Moulton and follow- ing him' by the Juege, on the question of flow at War- rington Bridge, which bad been gauged daily since 1894, intermittent gaugings having been taken between 1891 and the opening of the Ship Carel. A question arising as to the course to be taken with regard to the other affidavits, His Lordship said he thought there were two issues for him to try,and the first was whether,on the Ist of June, there would have been in the ordinary course of nature not less than 100 million cubic feet of water flowing past Howley Quay. It seemed to him clear there was not only not that, but that there was a great deal less, and less by more than the ten millions which would have been the ordinary flow. Was that caused by the works of the canal or by something else ? At present there so ,nted to him no reason to think that it was by any other means than the canal, and he suggested that the evidence should go to that point. Mr. Moult m said they hoped to show that there had been no breach of the injunction. They were not to divert more than ten millions, and he should prove beyond controversy that they had not diverted from the river Mersey running into the canal anything like ten millions. Whether any had disappeared in the bowels of the earth was another matter; but the Company were only answerable for not diverting, and he should prove that they bad not disobeyei the order of the Court, because they had not diverted the quantity they were allowed. , The learned counsel having asked and obtained per- mission to ask Mr. Hunter, the engineer to the Canal Company, a question on the flow of water through a feeder to the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, he said it , Ivoaori,oedoofreoumbideayfeteot day, d, and was The Company never had never more than about ex /Acted as much as ten millions a day. eo nd eoffe ntdhaellrt having Company's di. d not been supported by the evidence. It had been agreed that ittot ordere" d, t htohef natth est thcaetoiaunsrgste hrt thai r. they were entitled caseeb y e cis Mu the bo mu to take ten million fee:, whatever might be the flow, large or small ; and t a question to be considered was not the quantity lef t,but how much had the Company in any twenty-four hours abstracted or diverted for canal purposes. Their case was that they had never taken as ritch as they were allowed. Mr. Cripps was heard on the same side, quoting the records of the Company bearing on the flow and abstrac- tion of water. His Lordship said the question to be decided was one of fact—namely, whether the defendant Company had committed a breach of the injunction not to abstract more water than the Act permitted. There was no question of law in it, nor one of construction, though to make the case understood constrection came in in a limited way—the Company were never to divert more than ten million cubic feet of water in any twenty-four hours. As a fact, then, had they exceeded this? He had the evidence of Mr. Longdin, whom he bad had the advantage of seeing and questioning in the witness-box, not to say that be occupied a public and independent position, which made his testimony the more valuable. On the evidence, extending over some years' observe- tion, he found that whereas the minimum flow of water passing Warrington Bridge before 1893 was 70 million cubic feet, in the present year it was about 354 millions. The Medical Officer of Health (Mr. McDougall) re- ported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 13. There were no inquest cases. Of the 13 deaths two each were due to pneu- monia, infantile diarrhoeii, infantile convulsions, con- genital debility, and one each to heart disease, cancer, phithisis, tubercular diee' se of the bowels, and obstruc- tion of the bowel. The 13 deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 84. Forty-two births were registered.

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION SPECIAL COMMITTEE. The committee appointed to confer with the Runcorn School Board on the advisability of providing secondary education for the town beg to report that they have met the members of the said Board, and alter carefully con- sidering the matter,it wds resolved to submit the follow- ing resolution to the Council :—" That this conference is of opinion that it is not practicable for the Runcorn School Board to hold a Higher Grade School in the Tech- nical Institute because of the requirements of the Educ- ation Department involving structural alterations, pro- vision of a playground, &-t.,and that the only practicable scheme before them is that of the Secretary of the Tech- nical Instruction Committee,viz.the establishment of an Organized Science Day School and Commercial School. The conference beg respectfully to urge the Runcorn Urban District Council to request their Technical Instruction Committee to consider and report as to the feasibility of such a scheme or to formulate a fresh one." Mr. Wiswall, in proposing the adoption of the above minutes, said there was some little confusion over the resolution and voting at the conference between the Technical Instruction Committee and the School Board. In his epinioc the resolution ought to be altered.He pro- posed that it should read : "That this conference is of opinion that it is not practicable for the Runcorn School Board to hold a higher grade school in the Technical Institute because of the requirements ef the Education Department involving structural alterations, provision of a playground, kc., and that the only practicable scheme before them is the establishment of an organised science day school and commercial school. The con- ference beg respectfully to urge the Runcorn Urban Dis- trict Council to request their Technical Instruction Com- mittee to consider and report as to the feasibility of such a seheme.'i He moved that this be submitted to the Technical Instruction Committee in the form that be had read. He was prepared to give reasons, and to answer any questions on the subject. It was a grave matter and required their most careful consideration. Mr. Wilson seconded and the minutes were carried.

THR TRADES' COMMITTER.

Mr. Speakmdn said the Trades Committee since its appointment had been working very assiduously, and with good results. It was very satisfactory for them to knew that they had a very full committee when they met the other day, and he believed the committee would continue to ben fruit. In reference to the question that they were asked at the last meeting, he took it that the town was not suffering so much from real depression,as from the great amount of talk that had been going. the rounds that the town had been in a depressed :ate. Re thought it very unwise that these things shoulit get into the newspapers as it endangered the prospects of their town very much. He had information that morn- ing that 36 vessels were coming into Runcorn with clay alone. It was quite difficult to bear depression, but it was very much harder when people were always talking about the depression and making things worse, instead ,of trying to mend them. He was talking to one of the largest grocers in the town, and he said trade was dis- tinctly better. If they went on and said things were worse,they;would stop peopla coming into the town. He wished to give a warning voice to those people who were always crying about the town's depression. The railway rates they bad got down to a decent level, and the trades' committee new complained that they were too low,as the inhabitants took their money and spent it in other towns.-IThe Chairman said they were all glad (to hear that the Trades' Committee were doing good work. He thought there was some truth in the matter, of the people crying out and making depression worse. So far as empty houses were concerned he remarnb•ral the time when an agent had the keys of 150 empty houses. Since then the trade had gone up,and it would go up again. This concluded the business.
AN INTERESTING CM.E TO FARMERS.

At the'Runcorn County Court on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Floulkes, an action was heard in which Frederick Weir, farmer, Whitley, sued Thomas Lowe, farmer, Norton for £24 35., being the amount due for manure sold and delivered at defendant's farm Norton. Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor of Warrington appeared for the plaintiff, whilst Mr. Durandu, barrister of Liver- pool appeared for the defence. Mr. Browne said the clainViwas for balance of accounts for manure on a farm arNorton, of which the plaintiff was the outgoing tenant and the defendant the incoming tenant. His client's tenancy expired in May last and he accordingly left on the farm the manure. The incoming tenant, or the landlord, was bound to take it, and Mr. Weir should receive two-thirds of the value of the manure. A meet- ing was arranged to take place, and it resulted in the manure being valued. Mr. Baxter who is well-known in the county for valuation business between outgoing and incoming tenants was appointed. Mr. Baxter was a friend of both parties. He valued it and put it down at £24 3s. Both parties were satisfied to have Mr. Baxter as the valuer. Now the plaintiff said it was too little, and the defendant said it was too much. His client had been offered £2O by Mr. Robinson, father-in- law of the defendant, but he refused to have it. Mr. Durandu said there was no agreement on his client's part to buy, and there was no debt. Frederick Weir said he formerly kept a farm at Nor- ton, under Sir Richard Brookes. He quitted it in May. The defendant succeeded him. He left some manure on the farm, he also left the settlement of it in his father's hands. - -

After a good deal of evidence had been given, his Honour atter summing up ac some length, thought it would be better if the parties could come to an arrange- ment between themselves. The parties here left the Court, and after about ten minutes' absence returned, and said they had made an arrangement. His Honour then dismissed the case.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THußsDAy.—Before his Honour Judge Wynne Vfoulkes. CLAIM FOR THE RETURN Or A GREENGROCER'S LURRT. —John Lightfoot, greengrocer, Lower Walton, claimed from Joan Taylor, his brotherin-law, the return of a lurry belonging to him which he alleged he wrongfully took away from his premises at Lower Walton on the 9th July, or its value £9; also the return of a pair of scales and a numher of weights belonging to him which he alleged the defendant wrongfully took away from his cart at Stockton Heath on the 11th of August, or their value £llos., and also damages for wrongful detention of these chattels amonnting to £5 15s. The defendant made a counter-claim for the return or value of certain articles,the property of defendant,value £5 18s. 6d and also £2 for detention. Mr. A. Browne represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Longland defended.—Mr. B6wne in stating the case said the plaintiff was a greengrocer at Lower Walton and the defendant was brother to the plaintiff's wife. When the plaintiff lived at Preston Brook,the defendant came and lodged with him. Some time afterwards the defendant suggested that the plain- tiff should leave his employment at Preston Brook and go to Lower Walton where he had started a greengrocery business. The plaintiff and his family removed to Lower Walton,and the defendant provided the capital for the business and paid all the expenses of the house. But the defendant never gave the plaintiff any wages at all. After working 18 months for the defendant, the plaintiff told the defendant that he could not go on any longer with- out wages, and gave the defendant notice to leave his house. The defendant stayed at the house under notice for three weeks, and then told the plaintiff that he would give him a start in business and give him a lurry, weights, and scales, and other things together with £3. The defend- ant gave the things, and when the plaintiff had used them for about twelve months the defendant came at midnight and took the lurry away from the plaintiff. The plaintiff proceeded with his business,but on the 11th August, when he was hawking at Stockton Heath, the defendant came and took the scales and weight and fish knife from the plaintiff's cart. His (Mr. Browne's) client contended that the 'defendant gave the things to the plaintiff instead of money. They denied the counter- claim.—The plaintiff gave evidence in corroboration of Mr. Browne's statement. The defendant gave him 8...3 in money at the Central Station. In cross-examination the plaintiff said he had the lurry in his possession for about ten months. The defendant gave it him on the 10th July. He denied that he took money from the drawer to provide himself and family with clothing when working for the defendant. He never told anybody that the defendant had lent him the lurry and other things. He painted Taylor's name out on the lorry about a fort- night before the defendant left. Witness put his own name on. The things were not left with him as a mat- ter of convenience. The lurry was worth about £9. The defendant made them a small allowance.—Mary Lightfoot, wife of the plaintiff, and Alice Lightfoot, daughter of the plaintiff, and Joseph Ward, engine driver, Lower Walton, also gave evidence. The latter stated that the defendant told him that he was going to leave the plaintiff the lurry and the tackle with it for the sake of the children.—Miss Ward also gave corrc bo- rative evidence. At this point of the case, His Honour asked whether an amicable settlement could not be arrived at. Mr. Longland consulted with his client but he declined to give the plaintiff the lurry. Proceeding with the case, Mr. Longland said his instructions were that the lurry never was given, but the defendant simply left it with the plaintiff for conven- ience. If it had not been for some unpleasantness between the parties no claim would have been made for it. The money taken in the business was put in a drawer, and the plaintiff and his wife made use of it for their personal requirements. The defendant was not indebted to the plaintiff for anything. He was surprised when the plaintiff claimed the lurry as his awn. On being asked for its return, the plaintiff refused to do so, and accordingly the defendant fetched it.— John Taylor, greengrocer, Lower Walton, the defendant, said the plaintiff was in the business with him. He gave the plaintiff any money he required. He left the things with the plaintiff when he was leaving because he had no place to put them. He first noticed that the plaintiff had removed his name from the cart about three months afterwards, and he asked the plaintiff why he had done so because the lurry did not belong to bia2.—Mr. Rough_ sedge and Mr. Dallow then gave evidence for the defence. Mr. Dallow stated that the plaintiff told him that the defendant had only lent hin2 the lurry. His Honour said on the evidence of the two witnesses named Ward, he must come to the conclusion that it was a gilt and not a loan so far as the lurry was concerneds He would give judgment for the plaintiff for the return of the lurry, scales and weights, and £2 for detention with costs. He also gave judgment for the plaintiff on the counter-claim. CLAIM FOR THE RICOVERT OF A WATCH CHAlN.—Joseph Dearden, 2 Vitriol-square, Earlestown, labourer, claimed from Sarah Jane Kynaston,a married woman, 451 Eden- field-road,Norden near Rochdale, the sum of £6 155., the value of a chain' and costs. Mr. Longton, solicitor, re- presented the plaintiff,and Mr. A. Molesworth, of Roch- dale,defended. In 'stating the case,Mr. Longton pointed out that the plaintiff pawned a chain,value £6, at Mrs. Thorpe's, Earlestown, for £2. It remained in pawn for about a year,and Mrs. Thorpe sent word to the plaintiff that he had better redeem it as she was giving up busi- ness. The plaintiff went to his brother-in-law named Kynaston and applied to him for money to redeem the chain. Kynaston agreed to advance the money, the chain was redeemed, and Mr. Kynaston kept the chain on behalf of his brother-in-law until such time he could repay him the amount advanced. Kynaston had since been separated from his wife, and when she left him she took with her the chain in question, and his client now clahned its recovery.—Joan Dearden, Vitriol-square, Earlestown, corroborated his solicitor's statemeat.—ln cross-examination he admitted that it was over three years since his brother-in-law redeemed the chain. He had been unable to repay the amount advanced. He denied that the action was a piece of spite in consequence of the separation of Mr.and Mrs. Kynaston.—Marcha Ann Vearden,and John Kynaston, 133, Legh-street, Earlestown, also gave evi- dence in support of the plaintiff's case.—His Honour (to Mr. Longton) : You haven't proved that the chain was in the possession of the defendant.—Mr. Longton: I will call her.—Mr. Molesworth : You must first pay her exnenses.—His Honour : Mr. Longton is entitled t) call anyone in court.—Mrs. Kynaston, the defendant, then entered the box, and st ated that the watch chain was in her possession for nearly four years. She had sold the chain but not since the separation order was granted. The plaintiff's wife told her that ehe could keen the chain, and that it consequently became her property. He pointed out that four years had elapsed since the chain was redeemed, and that the plaintiff had given up all ownership to it. The plaintiff's wife also told the defend- ant that she could keep it. His Honour said the plain- tiff's wife had no authority to do so, and he would give judgment for the return of the chain or its value.—Mr. Molesworth was about to address the Court again when his Honour said he declined to hear anything further. ALL ABouT A MEDAL.--John Kynaston, Earlestown, claimed from Sarah Jane Kynaston,Norden,the recovery of a medal or its value as. Mr. Longton appeared to support the claim, and Mr. Molesworth again defended. —Mr.Longton said the claim was for a medal value 15s. which his client set much value on. The two parties had been separated, and on the day the case was heard at Newton Sessions, the defendant was wearing the medal which was attached to her watch chain. After the magistrates' decision the defendant took the medal away with her. It had never been given to her.—Jehn Kytaaston corroborated his solicitor's statement.—ln cross-examination he denied that he gave his wife the medal three years age for a present.—Mrs.Kynaston was again called by Mr. Longton, and stated that her hus- band gave her the medal.—Mr. Molesworth said his de- fence was that the medal was a present.—His Honour expressed a wish to see the medal, they were sometimes highly prized.—Mr. Longton : Turkish medals are not much value, your Honour. (Laughter.)—His Honoar, after inspecting the medal, said he should call it a cross. He thought it was not likely that her husband would give a thing of that kind away, but more likely that he would lend it her. He would give a verdict for the re- turn of it, but eaeh party must pay its own costs.

QIJOITING MATCH. At Northwich, on Saturday, there was a large attendance to witness a quoiting match between Lewis Blackburn, of Winsfurd, and James Brice, of Warrington. Both men are acknowledged tip- toppers at the game, the former of the two being the runner-up to the Cheshire champion. The stakes at issue were £2O, and a great deal of betting took place on the result. The conditions agreed to were: --18 yards pitch, stiff clay,Bin. quoits,and 61 points up. The game was closely contested throughout, the men being level Itt 15. At 00 Blackburn led by a single, alter which be drew away and won at the finish by 19 points. Scores :—Blackburn,6l Brice, 42.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,

I wish Lo express my full satisfaction to all the voters for the kind and courteous way I have been received amongst you during the whole of my canvass, No one could have been beitertreated. I beg to return my sincere thanks to the 331 Electors who so kindly and truthfully carried out their promise by recording their votes in my favour on Monday last. I had just 700 votes faithfully and honourably Promised, but by some means, and it would appear at almost the last hour, 319 of them were induced to unfaithfulness ; still believing as I do that they were honest in 'promise and possibly to some extent pardonable foe weakness I thank them just the same, but hope the lesson may bear fruit in future loyalty.
I also thank my numerous friends and workers, who not only volunteered their help but who eo energetically laboured with and for me throughout the Election. I am yours faithfully, HENRY THORNTON.

THE GAMBLE INSTITUTE, ST. HELENS.
OPENING CE MONY.

On Thursday the Earl of Derby performed the cere- mony of formally opening the new Gamble Institute at St. Helens, witich is to serve the double purpose of a public library and technical school. The new building is of imposing dimensions, and occupies a fine site close to the 'Towist.Hall. The erection is of bright red brick, with elaborate terra-cotta facings. It consists of a base- ment ad three storeys. The ground floor is devoted to the purposes of the library,and includes a noble reading. room, with 400 yards of floor space. The basement in- cludes engineering, building, plumbing, and metallurgi- cal departments; the first floor has a physics lecture theatre, cookery and laundry-room, and a number of classrooms; awl the second floor has a chemical lecture theatre, a splendid laboratory, two large art-rooms, and a clay modelling-r)oin. The whole building, with the site, is the gift to the town of Colonel Gamble, C. 8., &c., who has been for half a century a prominent resident in the borough. The streets yesterday were gaily decorated, and the inhabitants observed almost univers-1 holiday. The local volunteers mustered strongly, and lined the streets leading to the Town Hall and Institute.

BAPTIST CHAPEL, GOLBORNE-STREET, On Sunday evening the Rev. J. T. Schoticld,the newly app.ointed pastor of the Baptist Church, Golborne- strebt, preached on " The Lord's Supper." In the course of his discourse the rev, gentleman remarked that there were many people in these enligh- tened days who would have us believe that the bread and the wine of the ordinance were the actual body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ. Such people took a figurative statement liLerally, but why did they not deal in a similarly literal manner with such passages as "I am the true vine," "1 am the door," &c. The fact was, such literal rendering of figurative expressions was absurd, and the doctrine of transubstantiation reduced the Lord's Supper to the level of mere conjury. It was said that the change in the elements was a mystery—a miracle—but he urged that in the case of the blind man receiving sight and the turning of the water into wine, there was ocular evidence of the miracles, whilst in regard to the Lord's Supper, the senses of tonch, taste, and smell testified that no change of any kind had taken place. Again, the Lord's Supper was not a means of salvation, and lie would refuse to administer the ordin- ance to any dying person, .as he preferred to leave the soul of such person alone with its God. He referred to the practice of administering the sacrament to the dying in the belief that such persons were all right if they par- took of it, and said the practice led to a great deal of harm, as he had known the sacrament administered to people of wicked lives. He proceeded to point out that the Lord's Supper was not intended to be divided—the bread far the laity, and the wine for the clergy. He believed that ev-.47 believer in Jesus Christ was a priest, and was entitled to partake of both the elements. He commended the sacrament as a real communion of the saints, and expressed his conviction that it was the sweetest of all the services God's people attended.

Witness went to see Mr. Hewitt, and he told witness that he hid no" seen the mare professionally for two vears.—lnspector Bilson. R.S.P.C.A.. said he examined the msre. The fetlock joint was completely rotteri.—The defendant said the animal had been passed by two inspectors of the society. He was fined 20s. and costs. _ _ .

Let us send you, free of charge, a pamphlet about the cod-liver oil industry of Norway. It is eieht tine ene half inches deep, six inches wide, and contains sixteen pages besides the cover. It is ca'l ‘d " Progress of the Century," and is illustrated with thirtv-two half-tone views of Norway scenery obtained by a snscial repre sentative sent to Norway for special information ablut the famous coq-fisheries of that picturesque country.

The pamphlet is instructive as well as interesting. It tells how cod-liver oil is made, its peculiar properties, the history of its use, and how al:nost by chance the medical profession discovered one of the most valuable substances known to modern sciencei. The pamphlet also reveals many facts about this wonderful product which are not generally known. For instance, it tells why cod-liver oil so often has a rancid taste aud how this taste may be avoided. It relates, step by step, the devolopment of this wonderful oil, and why it has been ffenerafiy adopted by physicians throughout the whole civilised world.

"Progress of the Century "is well worth reading whether there is any likelihood af your ever needing cod-liver oil or not. The cover is illustrated with group of Norway scenes, and one of the most striking pictures le one of the midnight sun, taken with an ordinary four by five camera. Many have failed in their etTlrts to photograph the sun at midnight. If you are interested in amateur photography the illustrations alone are worth your name on a post-card.

You need not send stampi for postage, or take the trouble to write a lettr. If you simply write you name and address plainly on a post-card we shall under stand that you would like to see this half-tone pamphlet and we shall be pleased to forward it to you. On Saturday Warrington journeyed to Widnes, taking eitb them about 1,500 supporters. Consequently there vas a good attendance of about 5,000 spectators on the aome ground. The weather was bright and clear, and admirably suited to the game. Both teams had their lest men on, and were as follows :—Widnes : Batey,full , lack; Brennan, Nevitt, Rispan, and Jones, three- quarters: Drummond and Alford, half-backs; El and- ley, Donnelly, T. Acton, J. Acton, Harnpson. Emery, Travis, and Grace, forwards. Warrington: Heesom, iull back ; Lawless, Cross, Barber, and Radford, three- quarters; Bate and Houghton, half-backs; Nevins, Taylor, Scholtze, Roby, Barrett, Swift, Meacock and forwards. • Widnes won the toss and elected to play with the mind in their favour. Ellll kicked off for Warrington and Taylor charged the return down. Nevitt put in a strong kick and Heesom was tackled without getting Ira hia return. Houghton got the ball away and passed to Barber, and the latter found- touch. in a good position. Another scrimmage gave Drum- ' moad a chance, and he gained ground by his kick. Cross was well tackled by Nevitt and immediately after, Warrington were penalised. Barber caught the ball and transferred play to half-way. A series of scrimmages followed, both sets of backs putting in some good kicks, but the homesters were not to ba denied and they epeedily reached Warrington 25 flag. Heesom was again tackled and from the scrimmage the ball was kicked over the Warrington line and a race between Jones and Law- less proved very exciting. The Warringtenian managed to save the try however. Still tha homesters kept on the offensive. and Drummond initiated a amart bout of Passing. The ball went in touch near the line. Alford in- etead of throwing the oval out dodged round the War- rington backs and grounded behind the posts,the visitors meanwhile appealing. Referee Kennedy allowed the tiy and Alford easily converted. This unlucky reverse ' seemed to demoralise the visitors. After a brief visit to the Widnes end, Houghton got off side, and Batey taking the penalty dropped a 'splendid goal from near the halfway line. As soon as the garne was going again Brennan was tackNd on the lake and Drummond essayed a drop. Play was danger- misly near the Warrington end, and Rispan securing (indeed Radford easily, and scored another try. Batey made a good attempt at goal The next minute a line out was formed on the visitors' 25, and Drummond kicked towards the Warrington line instead of throwing the ball. The Widnes forwards rushed up, and Tom Acton scored an easy try, Alford again converting. All this occurred in a few minutes from the start. Hill started °nee more and Barber just saved a certain try. Still there was no holding Widnes back, and Cross only just managed te upset another good passing movement. War- rington then had a look in, and some neat exchanges enabled Radford to reach midfield where he was tackled. A geed dribble almost sent Lawless over, and Barber had exceedingly hard lines in striking the upright with a drop. The visitors were now showing better combination, and another series of brilliant passes put Lawless in possession, and he crossed the line at the corner with a fine spurt. Taylor failed to convert. Half time arrived with Widnes leading by 3 goals (1 penalty) I 1 try, to a try. Alford kicked off and Houghton retured. Bate gained ground and Taylor was effectively tackled. Barber kicked in touch at a critical moment. Rispan essayed a drop at goal which failed, the ball passing close to the posts. The homesters looked dangerous and another of Barber's well-judged kieke proved welcome. Bate and Taylor made a break which carried: the game to mid- field and Cross got away. Lawless followed up well but was tbo far forward to take the pass when a try seemed certain. Baty tackled Barber and a moment later nee. vented Heughton getting over, hy a kick ia touch. War- rington were now close to the Widnes goal and a pass. from Houghton te Bate and then to Lawless saw the lat- ter notch another good try. Taylor made a poor at- tempt at goal. After this Widnes got the upper hand and nearly got over on two occasions. Time arrivei with the score reading, Widnes three goals (one penalty) one try (18 points) to Warrington two tries (8 points).

RUNCORN V. ST. FIRLENS.—This game was played on Saturday afternoon, at Knowsley-road, before a splendid gate—some 7,000. Consequent upon Runcorn's defeat at Morecambe the previous week their team had under- gone a moderate change. Several old players were missing,but a good team had been mustered. St Helens relied on the same team that beat Widnes so easily tile week before,but at the last moment Caveney took the place of Tom Winstanley, who was absent through sick- ness. Runcorn won the toss and Cross kicked off for St. Helens,and the visitors almost immediately pressed: Houghton was tackled with the ball at half way, and even play ensued. St. Helens were ac arcied a penalty. for obstructien,but little ground was gained,and Hough- ton ma&, a good return, but the homesters worked well up. Traynor and warder kicked well. Nice passing among the Runcorn backs again gained ground right up to the home line, where they struggled hard until they gained a minoe. From the drop-out -St. Helens worked to half way, where Lewis evaded all but Houghton. Shortly afterwards Foulkes made a fine save. Runcorn again pressed hard until Butterworth scored a try at the corner, but no goal resulted. From the drop-out even play occurred at mid-field, where Faulkner took a penalty kick, which RPM well-landed into tench as mid- fi .Id by Archer. Runcorn secured repeated possession from the scrimmages, but couli not always get away. Grose and Traynor played well and got the hall away, but Runcorn plarrd strong iti d'jence, when Warder gap got well away, but the chance was lost by a pass for- ward. BUtterworth then dropped a erand goal. Half- time :—Runcorn seven points ; St. Helens nil. On re- sumine, the home team went at it dine-Jong, and Briers going down the field with the ball at his toes made an opening. for Archer, which was not taken, but a few moments later Cross gave his left-wing a long pass, enabling him to slip over easily at the corner flag. O'Hara veal the most prominent player on hisside at this point. fle:rn vie a fine sprint, and finished up with a pass which_ wmi mulled, and then charged down Myer's kick almosc under the Runcorn posts, the ball bouncing luakily into Houghton's hands. Briers dribbled prettily past the Rlncorn full back only to see the ball strike the '25" flag stick, and even when Warder rniskicked tn- wards his own line, and the ball dropped in the midst of half a dnz-n S. FiAPnq forwards, with nary a Runcorn man within y,ir is, it wfts a case of too many cooks spoi'- ing the brotti. Ton en I soon came—no q iickly for the home supporters—and Runcorn were adjadged the win- ners of a had and exciting game by a dropised goal and 3 try to a try. k

Ridgway for .fiVe years. He had known the prisoner personally when he (Mr. Davies) lived in Penketh. Mr. Swift said it had come out in evidence more em- phatically than he had anticipated it would do that Mr. Cross gave the prisoner the money. His evideuce could not be shaken. He said he gave the prisoner the money, and Molyneux had not wavered a bit fr3rn what he said in the police court. If the jury said that Mr. and Mrs. Cross were not telling the truth, and if they had any doubt in the case,the prisoner was entitled to the benefit of that doubt. They must not lay too much stress upon a good character. He did not deny that the prisoner had a good character,but every man had a good charac- ter until he lost it. That might he the prisoner's first slip,but the mere fact that up to the present time he had borne a good character was no reason why he should be acquitted for the present charge. He con- tended that he had proved the case up to tke hilt, and if so it would be the duty of the jury, however painful it might be, to fin..l him guilty. Mr. Harrison also addressed the Court, and said his frien I Mr. Swift had conducted the case not in a funereal manner, but a bloodthirsty manner time would have done justice to the gentleman who had been pursuing tke Armenians. (" Oh, oh, and laughter.") Apart from suggessions of that character, however, this was a very serious case indeed for the poor old man. He was 70 years of age, and had borne a good character all his lite. Mr. Davies had spoken very highly of him, and the police had also given him as good a character as a per- son could have. The law did not allow, as it now stood, the prisoner to open his mouth or to go into the box, or he would do so. It would not allow him to say what occurred. He had from the first denied the offence. When charged by the police with the robbery he said, "I am innocent," and that was his defence that day. He contended that it had never been proved that the money was han'eled over to the prisoner. Would the man forfeit his character for the sake of £5?

The jury, after a short deliberation, found the pri- soner guilty, but recommended him to mercy on account of his previous good character. Mr. flarrisen said his application, made in the other court earlier in the day, was for an adjournment to en- able him to call further witnesses as to prisoner's char- acter. Telegrams had been received from a gentleman to say that he could give evidence in the prisoner's favour on the following morning. The Chairman: We are quite prepared to believe he has a good character, and we also take into considera- tion the recommendation of the jury. Taking all the circumstances of the case into consideration, the Bench have decided to pan the lenient sentence of 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour.
