THE OnLBOHNE WOUNDING CASE. Abel Pirnh'ett, Edge Green-lanc, Gothorns (21), a cot. Her, was charged with having, on the sth September,at Go'borne, maliciously wounded Ann Roberts. The com- plainant is a married woman, and on the night In ques- tion, at half-past eleven, she saw the defendant. He was in her yard oriel was looking through the back kitchen window. He first of all broke a broom and threw it into the house, and than burst open the door. She did not do anything. He threw a large piece of mug at her. Ho also broke o large mug. Witness was in the kitchen. The defendant shouted to her, "Come out,you Charles Aunt,and I will kill you." The defendant then broke a lane mug. The mug was on a bench in the yard.-he went close to the kitchen door, and ha threw a large niece of mug, which hit her on the head. She saw the piece coming, but did not re- member anything else. She became insensible —Prisoner was committed to gaol for a month. James Carlon (24), collier, and Patrick Carney (26), also a collier, were charged with having at Golborn, on the 10th October, maliciously wounded Thomas Cooper. —The facts of the case have been reported at length in tho " Examiner."—Mr. Swift (instructed by Messrs. Greenall and Buckton) appeared for the prosecution ,and Mr. Collingwood Hope (instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw) represented the defendants.— Cooper, who is a miner, last employed in Australia, said he now resided with his brother at 17, Heath-road, Got. borne. A few minutes past eleven on S iturday nieht, the 10th October, he was going up Heath-street, Gol- borne. The two defendants and another man rushed at him. He knew Carney by name and by sight, but he did not then know either of the other two. The de- fendants lifted him up and threw him down, and Carney commenced to kick him on the top and left side of the head. The defendant Carlon got on the top of him,held him down, and commenced to bite his left ear. He bit it several dines. He (complainant) bled a good deal from the wounds on his head.—The Chairman having summed up the evidence the jury found the prisoners guilty, and they were committed to gaol for four months with hard labour each. Sir William character- ised the assault as a vc ry brutal and unprovoked one, and said the magistrates were determined to put down ruffi/nism in Golhorne.
THE ALLEGED THEFT FROM A WARRINGTON
BUTCHER.

Samuel Pomfrev (70), a labourer, living at Wright- street, Sankey Bridges, was charged in the second , court, before Mr, Marshall and other magistrates, with having at Warrington, on the 21st October, " then being the bailee of a certain sum of money, to sy:t £5, the moneys of one John Cross, did fraudulently teke and convert the same to his own use,and thereby feloniously did steal the same:" Mr. Rigby Swift (instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne) .‘appeared for the prosecution', and Mr. Harrrison (instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw) for the defence. Mr. Swift opened the case, from which it appeared that on the 21,t October Mrs. Crees had to pay a tra- veller who was coming £5, and M. Creels was to send the money in gold. He had no gold and took defendant with him to a pawnshop, of which Mr. Briggs is the manager, to get some gold for his silver. He got the gold and put it in a bag in the presenee of Mr. Briggs. He then delivered the money to Pomfrey, and was heard by one of the witnesses to tell him to "take it to the missis." Prisoner drove away in the direction of Liver- pool-road. It took him half an hour to reach the house, although it should only have taken him ten minutes. When he got to the house Mrs. Cross asked him if he had got anything, and he replied that he had not. She sent a note to Mr. Cross, and when he received it he asked Pomfrey what he had done with the money, and he at once denied that he had had any. Prisoner was taken to Sergeant Devlin's house and searched, but nothing could he found on him. The prosecutor said he was a butcher living at 220, Liverponcroad, Sankey Bridges, and he kept a stall in warringten market. He remembered Wednesday, the 214 t Cctober, On that day he got some money from his wife to be changed into gold (namely, £5). He had the prisoner with him in the trap when he went to Briggs's pa wnsh,lp to change the money, and from there he went te the market. He placed five sovereigns in bag, put it in Ids pocket, and went to the market. He gave the Prisoner the bag, and told him to take the money to Mrs. Cross. He saw him turn the pony round and drive , off. He was positive he gave tie:, prisoner the mrmev. fle afterwards received a note from his wife.—By Mr. ' Harrison : From first to last the prisoner had denied the theft. He had also denied it to Mrs. Cross. He first , of all after the robbery communicated with P.C. Due- dale, and afterwards with the Warrington police. The Chief Constable told him to apply for a warrant. Prisoner had lived in Sankey Bridges for a long time. He had borne a good character for anything witness knew to the contrary. His wife loeked after his shop in Liverpool- road on Wednesdays and Saturdays, when he (proftecu- tor).wae engaged in the market. When the prisoner se- turned from Sankey Bedges he asked him what he had done with the money which had been given to him, and he said he had no money. He (witness) had from time to time sent money to his wife by his assistants. Prisoner was in his employ. • Mary Cross, wife of the prosecute'', was next called. On the day in genestion she gave her husband £5 in Filver in the morning, and asked him to get it changed into gold for her, as she was expecting a traveller. He said he would do so and send the money back bv Pone. free.. When Pomfrey came to the house she ask,- I him if he had brought anything for her, and he replied, " I have brought nowt." ern Briggs, pawnbroker, said he gave the prose- er £5 in gold for £5 worth of silver. E iwin Molyneux, assistant butcher, said that on the 21-A of October he saw the prosecutor give Pomfrey a h4e to take to Mrs. Cross. The bag appeared to him to he very much like the bag now produced. He did not knew what was in it. div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

ST. ELTRIN'S BRIGADE V. WARRINGTON RAMBLERS.— This match was played on the ground of the first named club, on Saturday, the final score reading—St. Elphin's, three goals ; Ramblers, one goal. PENMETH V. ORFORD BARRACKS.—This match was played at Penketh on Saturday, Pen keth registering their first win this season. There was no score in the first half. In the second half the visitors were over- played, and in spite of a plucky defence, as the call of time Penkath were conquerors by six goals to one.

div.head: LOCAL CASES AT THE LIVERPOOL QUARTER SESSIONS.
div.p: LOCAL CASES AT THE LIVER- POOL QUARTER SESSIONS.

Several cases from Warrington and the district were heard at the Liverpool County Quarter Sessions, at the Sessions House, Islington, on Tuesday. There was a large attendance of magistrutes, over whom Sir William B. Forwood. presided.

div.head: THEFT OF CLOTHING FROM ORFORD BARRACKS
div.p: THEFT OF CLOTHING FROM ORFORD BARRACKS

William McGane (26), described as of imperfect educa- tion, was charged with having, at Warrington, on the 22nd October, stolen a coat, a vest, a pair of trousers, a muffisr, and 13s. 11d, in money, the property of Michael James Hanley and others. He was further charged witk having been previously convicted of felony at the assizes. —The prisoner pleaded guilty.—lt appeared from the statement of counsel that the prosecutor is an army reserve man, stationed at Orford Barracks, Warrington, and that on the evening in question he and prisoner went to bed in the same room at the barracks. The prosecu- tor hung his clothes on a peg close to the bed head. At half-past six the next morning he missed them, as well as an army reserve paper. Prisoner was also missing. Prosecutor, reported his loss to the military authorities, and prisoner was subsequently apprehended by the Warrington police on the charge of stealing, and cf.,m. mitted to the Sessions.—The Chairman said the prisc'ner was an old offender. He held a record of his past cv,•eer in his hand. It went back for a period of ten yrivis. MoGane had served carious terms of imprisonment for diff,rent offences, including burglary and shop-breaking. The last time he was before the Court was at the Liver- pool Assizes, when he received three years' penal servi- tude. The sentence of the Court on the present occasion was that he be imprisonei for nine calendar months with hard labour.

TNEFT OF BOOTS. Annie WhittakAr (45) pleaded guilty to stealing a pair of hoots on the 26th October, at Warringtcn, the pro_ pertv of Arthur Booth. She was sentenced to mine months' imprisonment, the Chairman remarking that she was a woman apparently of an incorrigible charac- ter.

div.head: HOW THE LIFE OF MR. WATSON WAS SAVED.

div.head: HOME-COMING OF MAJOR AND MRS. WALKER.
div.p: HOME-COMING OF MAJOR AND MRS. WALKER.
EN I'HUSUSTIC RECEPTION.

Midst the rejoicings of the villagers of Gateacre,Major W. H. Walker and his bride,after having spent an enjoy- able honeymoon trip on the Continent, arri sed at Gate- acre Grange on Saturday evening. Having travelled from London by the London and North-Western express the happy couple alighted at Mossley Hill Station shortly after six o'clock, where a carriage wan in readiness to convey the to Gateacre, and the scene that /0 et their gaze in the Grange geounds will undoubtedly ever re- main as a pleasant memory to both. Under the guid- ance of a committee of the residents,of sehicla the Revel. J. Sandy! was the chairman, elaborate prepaeations had been carried out in the vicinity of the house. At the entrance to:tlam grounds a large triumphal arch, com- posed of evergreens and bearing the words " Welcome " and " Happiness" had been erected, whilst a pleasing effect wee produced by the numer- ous fairy lamps of various tints which had been hung amongst the foliage aiong the carriage drive. In front of the main daor of the Grange, where, in ad- dition to the fairy lamps, several large torches illumin- ated the garden, the children, some 200 in number,from the Gatescro Schools, together with tha villagers, as- sembled, and as Major and Mrs. Walker alighted from the carriage they were greeted with enthusiastic cheer- ing and waving of hats and hankerchiefs. As the Maim. and his wife took up their stand in the porch, Florrie Ashe—a little schoolgirl of but six summers—handed to Mrs. Walker a beautiful bouquet of flowers, which was accompanied by a card bearing the words: With love to Mrs. Walker on her home coming, froth the children attending Gateacre Schools, wishing her and Major Walker a long, bright, and happy future in our midst. Presented by Florrie Ashe,Elsie Ja.ckson,Minnie Jackson, Alice Glover, and Annie Buttery." The school children then sang" Home, Sweet Home," And Mr. G. Hulatt read the following address, which was presented to Major Walker :—" To Major W. Hall Walker. Dear Sir,—On behalf of the inhabitants of the vi .ege of Gateacre we desire to extend to you atot to Mrs. W. Hall Walker a most warm and respectful welcome home. We venture to assure you that we are not forgetful of the kindlyinterest you have taken again and again in our village, and the good help you have even to every effort for its improvement and welfare. The Os, of your present home-coming is one which our respect and regard for you .induce us to celebrate, and our earnest wish woul tie to =masa that joy, if sech were posslble, by assuring you how sincerely we partici- pate in it. May the coming years but reveal to you and your bride new stores of health and happiness, anti may love and peace guard with such jealows care your home as to exalt and purify every jay, and to allow there no resting place for anxiety or sorrow.—Yours faithfully, John J. Sands (chairman), George Dale (honorary treasurer), G. Hulett (honorary secretary), Peter Jack- son, F. Boulton, J. !I..ltimmer, James Ashe, John M'llay James Glover, William Jackson, John Glover, James Wadsworth, John Bourne, John Blackburn, and J. A. Ga.teacre, 0 :tober 31st, 1896."—The address which was beautifully illuminated, was on a vellum scroll backed with white silk and attached to an ivory roller—Major Walker, in reply, said : My kind friends— The hearty welcome which you have ;lc ()Med me this evening, on the homr-eeming of my wife and myself, has affected ms very desplv. It is one which we indicates in the firstthappreciat place that deeply and never forget. I that you heartily approve of the choice which I have made in the future mistress of !say hoine—(cheers)—and that you wish to join with me in that joy which lam proud to feel it is my good fortune to possess. (Cheers) Secondly, your welcome this evening will show to my wife that I have amongst those who dwell here cenamaoded some respect. (Cheers.) I can only assure you that I shall always be pleased to assist those who, by their industry, assist themselves— (applause)—and in anything I can do to promote the welfare of the locality in which you dwell. (Cheers.) I have to thank you very sincerely for your hearty we. come this evening, also, on behalf of my wife especially, for the very beautiful flowers they have ptesented to her, and of course for the kind and generous words of your very considerate address ; and lastly, for the kind words that have been sung this evening—" Home,Swe et Home." (Loud cheers.)—Major Walker, who seemed deeply affected, then proceeded into the house with his wife, and the villagers dispersed.
HEAVY SENTENCE ON A WARRINGTON BOXING- MAN.

Themes Walsh, rsaid to be a Warrington boxing-man, was charged at Liverpool on Satur- day on remand with having stolen, on the 160 alt., a gold watch, valued at £2O, from the person of John Williams. Prosecutor is a retired tobacconist, living in York-terrace, Netherfield-road, and the robbery occurred in the yard of a public- house in Scatland-place. The watch was sub-e- -quently pledged by the prisoner for £3, and this led to the prisoner's arrest the same day by Detective Gib:4on.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and there being a bad record against him, he was sentenced to four months' imprisonment.

div.head: 'GIRLS' FRIENDLY SOCIETY.
div.p: 'GIRLS' FRIENDLY SOCIETY.

An entertainment in connection with 'll9 St. Paul's branch of the G.F.S., which was en? -lei, in 1879. and is one of the oldest single branches in tiw diocese of Liverpool, was given in the schoolroow on Monday evening. It was entitled "The G.P.S. in Great Britain," and consisted of a popular des- cription of the work of the society, with specially illustrated lantern slides. Songs and recitations were given. The lecture was read by the Vicar (the Rev. H. V. Pigot). The lauternist was Mr. R. J. Chorley. Mr. K. Wilkes presided at the piano. Amongst the photograp'ii thrown on the screen,be- sides those of members of the Central Council, were Lady Latham, the president for the diocese of Liverpool, and St. Paul's Branch Secretary, Mrs. Pigot. The entertainment had taken some few weeks to prepare. au.' was undertaken by both as- ociateS and members.
SHIP CANAL.
THE COTTON TRADE AND THE SHIP CANAL.

A Manchester contemporary says :—The recent reduc- tions in the dues on cotton and grain at Liverpool do not appear as yet to have bad the effect of checking the growth of direct shipments to Manchester by way of the canal. On the contrary, there is every indication that the importation of both these articles from America and from Egypt will this season show a decided advance even upon We satisfactory record of last year. The season nominally began on September Ist, but the first arrivals of Mancheater cetton did not reach the Man- chester docks until the 26th of that month. Up to the present eight steamers have arrived with 13,006 bales of American cotton, the latest of these being the Luciria from New Orleans, and the Lassen from New York, which came into dock on Saturday. There are an addi- tional 8,286 bales afleat from Galveston, New Orleans, and New York. The Olbers, due about the 10th of this month, has on board one of the largest cargoes of Sea Island cotton ever brought to Manchester—the quantity being 1,300 bales—besides a full general cargo. The Flaxman is now on the berth loading for Manchester direct, and the Strabo will follow, each steamer having booked all the cotton space availablo. The fluntcliff is due to sail from. Mobile direct to Manchester with cot- ton and other merchandise, and further sailings from that port will, it is explessed, be shortly announced. Since September 16th, 5,985 bales of Eyyptian cotton have been landed trom Alexandria by three steamers, and there are now 4,793 bales afloat. The total quantity of cotton already di<charged at Manchester since the let September or actually afloat for the port is over 32,000 bales. This is, of course, exclusive of the cargoes that are booked for the steamers that have not yet loaded.

div.head: LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.
div.p: LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

During the wx...;ek ended Friday, October 30, 130 sea- going vessels, with an aggregate net registered tonnage of 42,254 tons, entered and cleared from the port of Man- chester, as against 103 vesscls, of 33,136 tons,during the corresponding period of last year. Thirty-eight vessels. of 24,881 tons, arrived from or cleared for for,ign ports, and 92 vesgels, of 17,373 tons, entered or left coastwise. Three barqus arrived with timber from Canada, and tw with dyewood from Central America ; two steamers arrived from Egypt and Syria with cotton and grain, two from the Me iterranean with fruit, one from Aus- trailia with frozen mutton, rabbits, aud wool, eight from the Continent with general merchandise and flints, one from Uleaborg with pulpwood,and one from Huelva with iron ore. Seven steamers cleared for France, Belgium, Holland, and Germany,four for the Baltic, and one each for Bilbao, Barcelona, Alexandria, and tiombay. Three barques cleared for Busier, Drammen. and New York respectively. One hundred and sixty-three head of cattle arrived from Dublin via the canal during the week. div.head: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
LIBERAL VICTORIES.

Monday saw the close of one of the most memor- able municipal contests which have taken place in Warrington. Both political parties placed eleven candidates in the field and strove hard for their re- turn. Yet, the election was quietly and dolorously conducted. Beyond the flitting about .of a few extra conveyances there was vet y little to indicate in the p incipal streets of the town during the early virt of the day that the battle of the wards was tuking place. In the vicinity of the polling booths, Mt.,. groups of people assembled, and a number of wor,. - z were doing their best to bring voters to the puii. The day throughout continued fine, and the canvassers were thus enabled to prosecute their work under favourable circumstances. At night. a change came over the scene, and the thoroughfares leading to the booths became e,•owded. The chances of the candidates were eagerly discussed, and as the time neared for the closing of the booths, there was a great deal of running about for electors who had not voted. At eight o'clock pre- cisely, the booths were closed, and the ballot-boxes were conveyed to the Town Hall as speedily as possible. The work of counting was proceeded with in the Council Chamber and the Mayor's Parlour, and all the results were known before ten o'clock. A large crowd assembled in front of the Town Hall, and in order that the time of waiting mightnass the more pleasantly,arrangements had been ma i e for the Borough Brass Band to play a selection of music. This was a pleasing innovation, and was appre- ciated by the spectators. The police arrangements were under the direction of the Chief Constable (Mr. L. Talbot) and were carried out in a satisfac- tory manner. The results were announced trom the Town Hall steps as soon as they were ascer- tained, but owing to the cheering of the spectato s very little more than the name of the winning candidate was heard. The results are appended, and as will be seer, six Liberals and five Conserva- tives are returned. This is a Liberal gain of three seats in the Council Chamber, and reduces the majority of the Conservatives—who hold eight of the nine Aldermanic seats—to six.

div.head: AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. SPEECHES BY SUCCESSFUL CANDIDATES AND OTHERS.
div.p: AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. SPEECHES BY SUCCESSFUL CANDIDATES AND OTHERS.

The Liberal Club was crowded to the doors after the declaration of the poll, and cheers and counter-cheers were rai;ed for the Liberal candidates. As the candi- dates arrived from the Town Hall they received an ova- tion, and it was some considerable time before quietness could be restored. Speeches were made in the large billiard room, the proceedings being presided over by Councillor William Pierpoint, the chairman of the Liberal Executive. On rising to speak the CHAIRMAN met with an enthu- siastic reception. He said he wished he could have com- plimented them upon a greater victory, but still he thought they had had some notable victories that day. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Shilicock had won Town Hall ward. He bad beaten a very good man, a very respectable man, and he was exceedingly sorry Mr. George Clay had not managed to win. Then Mr. Grace had beaten 'Mr. Thornton, and he did not congratulate the Torty party on their latest accession to their ranks. (Applause.) Mr. Grace was a young man with all his life before him, and he boned he would improve as ' time went on. (Applause.) He was , also sorry that their old and tried friend Mr. Joseph Mounfield had lost. He had been a most consistent supporter of the Liberal party. H had fought four hard fights and he (Mr. Pierpoint) believed be had lost in conse- quence of being maligned in reference- to trades union matters which had no foundation at all. (Applan,e.) They had in Mr. Strange a man who had worked, his way un by his own exertions to a position at compara- tive affluence. He was a man against whose moral character no stain could be placed. He was a man wha would have done well in the Council for Latchford, but in place of him they would now have Mi. Jolley. (Laughter.) Mr. Jolley might be a very good man in hi 4 way,but he believed Latchford had made a great mis- take in electing him. Mr. Jolley would not have been elected had it not been for that scurrilous placard which was issued,which was a disgrace to the Tory party. He was happy to say that stens had been taken in a legal form which would compel the printers of the placard to disclose the names of the authors of it, (Hear, hear.) Fairfield ward was dominated by the influence of the Church of England. That church had of course a per- fect right to use its influence in a legitimate way. The Liberals had &good man in the person of Dr. McCarthy, and he believed had it not been for the fact that Dr. McCarthy was an Irishman he would have been elected. If the Liberal party in Fairfiied Ward had been true, Dr. McCarthy would have been its representative and a very fit representative he would have been. (Applause.) Those were all the seats their opponents had wen. The first Liberal victory on his list would make up for a great deal of the disappointment they had met with, and that was the election of. Mr. Fleming for St. John's Ward. (cheers). Then he came to Bewsey Ward—(cheers)—a ward which he had al- ways looked upon as the strongest Liberal ward in the town, and which they lost last year through an =for- tunate split in their own party. (Shame) It had been won by a magnificent majority by their tried friend Councillor Shaw Green. (Cheers). The splendid victory of " Little Harry Roberts "—(cheers)—in, Wbitecross Ward showed very plainly that he was appreciated by all classes of the community, irrespective of party. (cheers). In St. Austin's. Ward they had not only. managed to secure the whole of the three seats, whieh was a most remarkable performance, but they had been the means of bringing back to public life in Warrington one of the best of her sons in the person of Mr. John Crosfield. (Loud cheers.) Dr. MCCARTHY in referring to his election in Fairfield Ward, said he had worked very hard, and if he was beaten he could not help it. (Applause.) He was not vanquished—(hear. hear.)—and he was willing to fight again. (Loud cheers). He thanked all his workers for the efforts they had put forth on his behalf. (Ap- plause.) Councillor TINN lON,WhO met with a hearty reception. said he stood before them in one of the proudest posi- tions be thought it was possible for any man in War- rington to occupy. (Loud cheers.) He was delighted that he had been placed at the head of the poll, and also that Mr. Thomas Burton and Mr. John Crosfield had been returned as his colleagues on the Town Council. (Cheers.) It was the result of hard work on the part of one of the finest ward committees any man had behind

THE SKIN IS COMPOSED of three layers, and con- tains muscles, nerves, blood vessels, lymphatics, sebace• ous glands. sweat glands, etc., while the hair and nails are its appendages. It is a most complicated piece of machinery, and sub:int, like any other organ, t. health and disease. To preserve the skin, scalp, and hair, and to restore them to a condition of health when diseased, nothing is so agreeable or so speedily effective as CCU- CUBA SOAP, assisted in the severer forms with mild ap- plications of CIITICURA (ointment) the great skia cure.

him. He felt that the returned candidates had had re- posed in them a trust for the next few years, and he hoped it had not been misplaced. (Applause.) He wished to thank everyone who had taken a part in the election in St. Austin's Ward. (Applause.) Mr. Ts:tomes BURTON, who was well received,in speak- ing of the proud position occupied by Mr. Tinnion at the head of the poll, said he had thoroughly earned it, and he (Nit. Burton) must congratulate him upon his succees. (Applause.) He could only confirm what Mr. Tinnion had said with regard to the splendid ward committee they had had in St. Austin's Ward. He had never seen men work so assiduously and untiringly, and he was thankful to the committee fnr the way they had conducted their work. (Applause.) He did not heeitat to say that their success had depended upon the energy of the workers. (Applause.) He ventured to say that they had fought an honourable battle—(hear, hear)— , and he would rather have an honourable battle and lose, than fight dishonourably and win. (Applause.) He was very proud that their three candidates had been elected to the Council. (Applause.) He hoped that his conduct in the Council weuld be such that the Liberal party coeld appreciate. (Cheers.) Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS, as chairman of the St. Austin's Ward Committee, said he was amply rewarded for any labour he had given as Chairman,by the glorious success they had had. (Loud cheers). He should not be dc- ine his duty to his colleagues on the Ward Committee 'if he did not especially name Mr. Tinnion for the mag- nificent work he had done. (Cheers.) If the Liberals had had good candidates all round as they had had in St. Austin's, he believed 'they would have had greater victories. (Applause.) Let them be of good cheer. (Hear, hear.) The future—the near future was with the Liberal party—(cheers)—and greater successes would before long be their good fortune. (Applause.) Councillor FLEMING, who on rising to speak was cheered again and again, said he wished to thank the workers in his ward for what they had done for him that day. If it had not been for them he would not have been in the proud position he now held. They had secured a great victory in St. John's ward—(cheers)— and he could hardly express his gratitude for the woik they had done. (Applause.) They knew what his past experience had been on the Town Council—(applause):— and he hoped to do in the future what he had done in the past. They had achieved a glorious victory, and he hoped it was the forerunner of greater victories in the same ward. (Cheers.) Councillor Saw GREEN who was loudly cheered, said for the fourth time he stood before them as a re- turned member of the Town Council. (Cheers.) For the past nine years he had tried to do his duty, and the magnificent victory that day—a victory of mete than two to one against them, spoke volumes for the stability and the strength of the Liberal party in Bewsey ward. (Applause.) He re-called three years ago, when they same into that room with two returned representatives against their opponents nine,and they then felt that if anything was to be done to retrieve the party,they must see to it by getting their organisations into a better posi- tion. (Hear, hear.) He did not think the: Liberal or- ganisation was ever so good as it was at the present time, and speaking for Bewsey ward, he could say it never stood better than that day. (Applause.) It had never worked harder. (Cheers.) It was said in Bewsey ward that his opponent was an independent Conserva- tive. (Laughter.) He noticed that the ink with which Mr. Aukland's address was printed was a deeper dyed blue than the rest,and if that was a sign of independence then he (Councillor Shaw Green) would like to know what was not. (Applause.) They had given Mr. Auk- land such a" slating" that day that he would not forget it for the !rest of his life. (Laughter.) It hadlbeen his (Councillor Shaw Green's) duty to report to the executive Committee how the ward was being worked by his opponent. For days and nights his opponent and his wife were about the ward canvassing and they came to the conclusion that Mr. Aukland never went home at all. (Laughter.) But Mr. Aukland had gone home now—(laughter)—and he hoped for good. (Loud laughter.) That morning to his intense indignation he saw being distributed in the ward handbills denouncing certain particulars in a circular which had been issued by his (Councillor Shaw Green's) committee,stating that he was the better of the two candidates. His opponent issued a handbill stating that the Chairman of the Liberal Ward Com- mittee had repudiated that circular and stated that lie knew nothing about it. But instead of doing him (Coun- cillor Shaw Green) harm it had done a power of good. (Applause.) In conclusion he thanked his workers for their untiring efforts on his behalf. (Applause.) Councillor HENRY ROBERTS who was greeted with a loud burst of applause. said he wished first of all to ex- press his sincere sympathy with those of their candi- dates who had not been successful that day. (Ap- plause.) He was not certain whether they v ould not have won two other seats had:it not beentfor the placard already referred to which had not only been circulated in the ward which it was supposed to effect, but all over the town, with the object of damaging the reputa- tion of the Liberal candidates. The authors of the placard would have an opportunity of proving their statements in the proper place. (Hear, hear.) He must thank his workers in Whitecross ward. They had always had a splendid reputation, and he thought they had exceeded it on the present occeeion. (Applause.) He must thank his lady friends for their help. They had worked untiringly from the earliest moment to the end, and while they had always polled a satis- fectory proportion of ladies in Whitecross ward, they had polled more that day than aver. (Applause.) He had been elected five times as a member of the Town Council. There were many apparently who did not consider him good enough for anything bettor than an ordinary councillor—(laughter)—but so long as the elec- tors ofithe Whitecross Wardichose to send him with such an emphatic decision as they:had done that day, he was satisfied with the position of an ordinary counelillor. (Laughter and applause.) He was rather inclined to think Mr. Battersby—(A voice: He's a dummy " laughter)--had been made what they called in Lanca- shire a mug of. (Hear, hear.) He thought the result of the Whitecrose election was satisfactory. (Laughter.) If it had been another hundred more it perhaps would have been better. (Cheers.) They might depend upon it that the election in Whitecross Ward was engaged in by the Conservatives with an object— that was to keep him (Councillor Roberts) and the ward committee busy, and preventing them from giving. assistance anywhere else. He was quite satisfied with the organisation of the Liberal party, and he did not think any candidate had lost through want of assistance from Whitecross ward. (Ap- plause.) Whether he (Counciller Roberts) would ever have an opportunity of a walk-ever he did not know and he did not very much care. (Laughter.) As long as the Conservatives chose to put up a candidate he (Councillor Roberts) would be there to fight him. (Ap- plause ) A Voice : "You will make his nose bleed." (Laughter.) Whitecross electors were not so short or intellect as to be deceived by a trades unionist in Tory colours. They were trades unionists in Whitecross ward,and as trades unionists they protested against one man undertaking two jobs. (Heir, hear.) A Voice : " Let Batteraby stop at the Post Office." (Laughter.) Although they had been defeated in several wards, they were encouraged by the magnificent return of their three candidates in St. Austin's ward—(applause)—and that went a long way to make up for deficiencies in other wards. (Applause.) They had that day received the unanimous support of the Irish electors in every ward. (Hear, hear.) -Re had not many Irish eiectois in his ward, but he was bound to say that every Irish- man in Whitecross ward had voted for him, and he les- lieved the same was a fact in every ward of the town. He was gratified to be able to Make that public testi- mony, and he was sure they would be pleased to hear it. (Anplause.) Mr. KIERNAN said Mr. Roberts bad not done the Irish- men of Warrington more than justice when he stated that they had been true to the Liberal party. (Ap- plause.) He was sorry the electors of Fairfield ward riad not put Dr. McCarthy in. It would have been in the way of a return for the services the Irish had rendered the Liberal party of Warrington. (Applause.) But he was only beaten by a small majority, and he hoped that the Liberal electors would support him on the next occasion. (Applause.) The Irishmen unanimously dr- cided to support the Liberal candidates, and he trusted Irishmen would get support in return. They formed one-seventh of the population of Warrington, and they were entitled to nne-seventh of the representation. (Hear, hear.) He trnsted Warrington would soon be able to return a Liberal representative to Parliament. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas MORRIS said they ought to feel somewhat proud of the result of the elections that day. (Ap- plause.) He was content with the return of six Liberals, and among them were some splendid fellows. (Hear, , hear.) Mr. THIRNTON, who was cordially received, spoke of the excellent work doneby .hia committee and also by some ladies. It was his opinion that if they had had double that number on the committee in Orford ward they could not have won owing to the evil forces against them. They were doing very well so long as they had daylieht, but when darkness came on-- (A Voice: "The devil was out." (Laughter.) He (Mr. Thornton) thought that gentleman was not far wrong. (Applause.) He had just as much pluck now as when the battle commenced. (Applause.) He would be there again to fight il'he was wanted. (o.ear, hear and applause.) The meeting shortly afterwards terminated.

div.head: AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
div.p: AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

After the declaration of the poll on Monday evening the leaders of the Conservative party adjourned to the Club. In the first-class billiard-room speeches were delivered by the successful candidates and others.' Mr. John White, J.P., said he was afraid that if they went into 'he matter minutely it would be found that they had lost more than they had won. He had,howevet, this gratifying intelligence to make known,and that was that in spite of the determined attack which had been made upon them this time all round—and the Liberals had played for all they knew—they still maintained their majority in the Town Council. They had a majority of six, which he thought, was a very good majority. They had certainly not lost owing to a want of good work. It had been magnificent in all directions especillly in the Howley Ward, where the majority was over 200. All the best candidates the Liberals could find

in the party had been brought out, and that was a cus- tom they usually adopted when they wanted to win. The fight had been fairly fought on both sides, and if it was the wish of some of the constituents that they should be lepresented by Liberals they must, as Conser- vatives, bow to that decision for the present. But they would never relax their efforts to win back the seats they had lost that day, and to maintain the ascendency they had in Warrington, because after all that had been said and done Warrington was still Conservative to the back- bone.

Mr. R .PIERPOINT,M. P. ,congratulated all present on the enthusiastic work which had been done. There had been enthusiasm running throughout the party all through the election. He regretted much that they had not more I congratulate themselves on than they had. In this ction they had everything to lose and very little to ga as the number of seats thep had to fight was very nc.. in excess of those which their Of, .nents had to h,nt. In St. Austin's Ward defeat had come upon them through the fact of so well-known and powerful a man as Mr. Jehn Crosfield having come out on the other side. —(A voice" What about the Local Veto.")—Continuing, Mr. Pierpoint said that not only in other wards but in the ward they were in, had excellent and enthusias'ic work been done, and they would forgive him if he said as the member-for the borough—(" Oh !")—that he was inclined to look upon these matters in what he hoped they would not regard a selfish light, namely,with regard to future Parliamentary contests. The work which had been shown that day was an exceedingly good augury He could not say that he altogether regretted that that contest would not lee until the 20% century had been well gone into. It was a fact that Warrington was Con- servative and they might count upon the Unionists. A good many however of the Liberal Unionists had not gone with the Conservative party that day they thought they had a right in municipal matters to vote for the party they used to be allied with. ("Shame.") He theught they were to be depended on at Parliament- ary elections notwithstanding. Alderman FRANCOMB said that all through the election there had been a true Tory ring, and with the exception of St. Austin's ward they had done remarkably well. If they had turned their thoughts to it they would have reversed the present figures. They might be defeated but they were not beaten. They had still a good majority in the Town Council of Warrington. Their late loader, Captain Reynolds.used to say 'Llot't get too big a majority in the Town Council because if 'von make blunders the Tory party will lose by it." Alderman Francomb thought they had no need to be upset because they had lost two or three seats as they could well afford to do so. The Liberals could have a seat or twc to cheer them up. Councillor BENNETT said he was proud to be in his position that evening, having been returned ter the Howley Ward by a majority of 204 votes. He was taunted three years ago with having been returned to the Council by a casting vote, but he thought they 1-ad very satisfactorily wiped out that taunt that night. He would now sit in the Council Cna.mber as the undis- puted representative of the ward. He should regard his position as a sacred trust. Councillor Lotearote said it would be remem - bered that last year Mr. R. I'. Fairclough lost the ward by 39 votes. On this occasion the Conservatives could rejoice upon having wen a glorious victory of 19 votes, the defeat of twelve months ago having been swept away. It was sufficient, and showed the ward to be of the right colour. Councillor GRACE said his heart was so full that he could hardly express the sentiments of gratitude which he felt towards the electors for having returned him as their representative. It was no easy thing to wipe out a minority ot 263 and to convert it into a majority of 73 in the short space of 12 months. He could mot take the credit to himself for such a successful result ; it was due to his noble band of workers. They had worked hard for him, and had shown that they had confidence in him. Last year they were not fighting a fair fight,but this year it was an honourable one. The ward was-not under the dictatorship of one individual • now as in the past.

Councillor SHILLCOCK, in returning thanks said that was the second time he had stood before them as the representative of the Town Hall IWard. His majority was greater !than had been received by any other representative of thelsard. Councillor JOLLEY was also called upon but did not respond.

div.head: PUBLIC-HOUSE ROW AT MARTINSCROFT.
div.p: A PUBLIC-HOUSE ROW AT MARTINS- CROFT.

WHOLESALE DESTRUCTION OF GLASSES, &c. On Wednesday morning at the Warrington County Petty Sessions before Mr. J. J. Bleckly and Mr. William Houghton, two General Post Offices employis William Scotusy and Francis Ellis were charged with having on the 26th of October been disorderly in the "horse and Jockey," Martinscroft, and refusing te quit ; they were both charged further with assaulting Nicholas Massey, the landlord; Scotney was charged in addition with breaking glasses and a jug, the property of Mr. Massey, and dping damage to the extent of ss. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted, and Mr. P. Davies defended. Mr. Browne said the defendants with a number of other men went into the Horse and Jockey on the day in question, and each had a p:nt of beer. Some of the men left, but the defendants and two other men re- mained. At the time the servant was cleaning the floor of the kitchen. Just as she finished Scotney commenced quarrelling, and adopted a threatening attitude to one of his mates. Massey told him to be quiet and Scotney then picked up a jug of beer and swilled it along the clean floor. Massey then ordered him out, and Scotney refused to eo and clinched his fist. Massey said he would send for the police, and Scotney said he did not care for all the police in Lancashire. The landlord then tried to put him out, and pushed him into the yard. Ellis came behind Massey and got hold of him reund the shoulders, and held him wUle Scotney went in again. Ellis threatened to tear Massey's eyes out, aad scratched him down the face. Two work- men came to the landlord's assistance. Scot- ney knocked a half-gallon jug down and broke it. They then wilfully smashed glass after glass and also broke some spirit decanters. To complete all Scotney took the chimney off a lamp and broke it with the remark " That is the way I break glass." Ha also smashed a whiskey glass and rushed at Mr. Massey with the jagged part in his hand. He was stopped by some painters present Mr. Browne suggested that if Mr. Davies would publicly apologise for defendants he would not preps the case. Mr. Davies said his instructions were totally different and he could not apoloeise.

Nicholas Massey,landlord of the "gorge and Jockey" corroborated Mr lirowne's statement.—ln cross-.exami- nation by Mr. Davies, witness denied that he nearly throttled Scotney in putting him out,or used any unduo violence.

Harry Welsby, painter, Mane.h ester-road, Warrington, deposed to seein- the defendants come in. They usei fr,ul lan:pine. Witness corroborated Mr. Massey's stato• ment. Massey's face was scratched, ire was not sure by whom.

Richard Gibbon, etated thet,he al3o was present. He supported the evidence for the niosecution. P.C. Heath denosedsto seeing Mr. Maesey's face. scratched. At the reel eest of complainant he took the names of the two defendants. He was taking another man's name when Ellis said he had nothing to do with it, " I have done it," meaning Ma.ssey'3 face. Mr. Davies, for the defence, pointed out that Scotney had hen employed by the Government for 12 years and was a steady, sober man. They had left Irlam early in the morning and reached Martinseroft abut two in the afternoon. Scotney had a drink of rum as he felt ill. The landlord charged him with having had too much drink and he then offered to go somewhere else. Massey then asked him to stay as he could manage another ane. He stayed, and when the landlord told him to go as ha thougSit he was rra‘king a row he said he had a right to his beer and threw it on the floor. He was going to the doer when the landlord caught hold of his scarf and draeeed him to the floor with it. Ellis then went to his mate's assistance, as he was justified in doiag. Mr. Davies contended that the glasses were broken ace.identp- Ally in the scuff!e between the landlord and Scotney. Both defendants he theught were justified, from the provocation received, in acting as they did. The defendant Scorner supported his solicitor's state- ment. He said he resided in Orford lane, Warrington, and had been an employe of the G.P.O. for 12 years. Ne added that the landlord dragged him by the loose end of his scarf. Ellis,who had not spoken up to then, went to his assistance. As a result of the struggle with Massey his (elcotney's) trousers were split and his knee cut. He absolutely denied smashing the lamp glass. Re never saw one in the place. The other glasses were ac- cidentally broken in the scrimmage. Ellis, the other defendant, also corroborated. After a short private consultation the magistrates dismissed Ellis on the charge of refusing* to quit and fined Scotney se. and costs. Far the assault on Massey both defendants were fined ss. and cost?, and for tl*e damage to elasses. Scotney was further fined is. and mete.
Mr. Browre was allowed an advocate's fee of one guinea and his witnesses' costs.

RUGBY FOOTBATZ.

Much depended on thP match et-tween Widnes and Warrington last Saturday as they are next to one another in the League table. Victory for Warrington meant them continuing their progress towards the top, while defeat on ibi2d Widnes to retain their strong posi- tion. Without this additional importance to the fixture the meeting between these two local clubs alwaysex- cites great interest in both towns. On Saturday theex- citement was immense, and about 1500 people accom- panied the W - ::on fifteen on their journey to Wiles. They travelled with a confidence of victory too, for itich improved form has been displayed of late that the War- rington players naturally thought they could etsly account for the Widnesians, who are somewhat disogao- ised. There was no change in the advertised team and at Widnes it was found that th homesters also had:heir full strength on.

One important fact, though not overlooked, was made light of in the Warrington prophecies of the result. That was the reputation of the Widnes team for winniag al- most every alternate match. "It's Widnes's turn to lose" or win, is (rite a common expression in Northern Union football circles. Last season the Widaesians never woe two matches in succession, and this season also they are upholding their character. A fortnght ago their neighbours at St. Helens inflicted a crushinj defeat upon them, so t 1.1.4 last Saturday it was their turn to win.; and win they did with a vengeance for belsre the game had been in progress a quarter of an hour War- rington had 16 points piled against them.

The first five points ought never to have bees Scored, and were but a forerunner of the ill-luck of the visitors allthe day. A line out well in Warrington quarters was the cause of it. Alford had possession of the ball, but instead of throwing it out fairly, he dodged round the Warrington backs without even bouncing the ball, and placed it behind the posts. No:one attempted to stop him, the visitors expecting that the referee would rule against it. Instead,however,the score was allowed and a goal being easily kicked, Warrington had 5 points against them, which they had no means of preventing. They seemed to lose heart for a time, while the home. sters were simply irresistible. Being penalised in midfield they were astcunaed to see Batev, the new Widnes full- back,drop a magnificent goal. Rispan:added a try soon after, and then five more points were given to Widnes by questionable tactics. Drummend from another line out, kicked instead of throwing, and the ball went over the Warrington line where T. Acton fell on is. The visi- tors were tricked, and unable to stop the try,which was converted. Thus 10 of the 16 points were not over much to the cr. of Widnes. Near the end of the first half Lawless ran in a really dashing try, and in the second half he succeeded in again scorieg cleverly. Neither try was converred, so that Warrington were,on the actual play,level with their opponents. Though the homeaters were superior in the first half, the visitors more than held their own in the remaining play.

Throughout the game, Batey, who cetnes from Tyne- dale, played a splendid defensive game for the home- sters. He is tall and powerful in build, so that WS tackling was not half-hearted by any means. Besides that he ran well, and kicked with excellent judgment. Not a fault could be found with him on Saturday's form. Heesom on the contrary was not quite up to the mark. Though very safe he was often tackled with the ball, and his kicks did not find touch so surely. The two pairs of half-backs were well matched, though the home twain secured some advantage from the superior energy of their forwards. The latter are a big lot and gave the visitors much hard work. The Widnes three-quarter line'showed quite unusual combination and dash. The men were about equal in merit.

Warrington were best represented bY Lawless and Barber. The former saved a certain try and scored twl others. Never was his dashing play seen to better advantage, and he was quite the smartest wing on the field. Barber worked untiringly and it is no exagger- ation to say that but for him the score would have been larger. Cross played his usual good eagle.

It is unpleasant to say anything in deterioration of the skill of any player,much' less a young one,but I can- not help but nommen': on Radford's weakness as wing three-quarter. Last Saturday he was completely out- elassed. The Widnes men played on him and as a re- suit Rispan was let in and scored. Often Radford proved quite incapable nf tackling and it was scarcely any use trusting itim with a pass. He has not vet had experience enough for.first class football, but he may in time make a really useful man. The committee have acted wisely in relegating him to the "A " team. Hig- ginbottona,as his successor, should be an improvement. His debut tc-lay as three-quarter will be watched with _interest.

To-day's match will be a stiff one and the chances seem against Warrington being victorious. Still they managed to thrash the Hornets and there is ao reason why they should not be the first club to lower the colours of Broughton Rangers. Let them work with a will and they should render a good account of them- selves.

Almost as much interest was felt in the match at Wilderspool on Saturday, when Widnes "A," the prev- iously undefeated champions of the junior league were met. Warrington" A "occupied second place, so that the contest was Greek against Greek. Several first tamers were in the visitors' ranks. The game through- out was fiercely contested and up to half-time there was no score. In the second half Higginbottom charged a kick down and obtained three points. Foden converted. Later on the tremendous efforts of the visitors resulted in them getting a try at the corner, but the goal kick failed. Warrington retired winners by 1 goal k 5 points) to a try (3 points). Both tull backs, Boscow and Gray- son played splendidly, buegthe home forwards were beaten. This told against the half backs but they worked hard, and the victory was all the more creditable. Wid- nes had hard lines on several occasions and were if any- thing the better team. Boscow was mainly instru- mental in keeping them out, while Higginbottom was the best back on the field.

St Mary's are still on the winning tack. Their last feat has been to administer a licking of a goal and a try to nil to the Runcorn Recs. Dakin was the first scorer and Roug,hley kicked a goal. Bennett notched the second try but Roughley could not add another two points. Like their friends, the Warrivlton "&," St. Mary's defeated a club which has hitherto this seas ma, carried all before it. Whatever may be said of the premier team, there are good footballers in Warrington yet.
Among them are the Loco's who made a mess of the floters from Frodsham on Slturdar br thrashing them to Vic, tune of 20 points to Ml. The Loco's with steam up are a sight to gee.

St. Helens supporters, were greatly suprised by the way Runcorn vanquished their team. Great interest was evinced in the match. as St. Helens easily wiped out Widnes the previous Saturday by a goal and three tries to nothing, and it was anticipated that the same fate would befall the cup-holders. It was even asserted in one of the Liverpool newspapers, during the last week that St. Helens with the aid of a new man who was expected to turn out for them, would have no difficulty in sending their opponents home defeated.
But the lesson learned by Runcorn the previ mis Satur- day at Morecambe is not to be forgotten, and in conse- quence a good team was put on to meet the glasbblowers.

When on the field both teams appeared to be in rare form. The visitors commenced the pressure, and soon had play under the homesters' goal post. Houghton was again in form and repeatedly saved his team a lot of work. The combined play of the visitors was also vastly superior to that of the honiesters.

At the conclusion of hostilities, St. Helens had a goal and a try (both scored by Butterworth) chalked up against them and a try to their credit—a fair beating. It would be wise if St. Helens relinquiahed the idea of predicting the winner in future.

Th‘s "A "team appear to carry all before them. ,pponent on Saturday was St. Helens" A." The game was fast and very interesting, the men acquitting themselves in grand style. At the interval a score of one goal and two tries to St. Wiens nil was entered, down. The second half like the first was in favour of Runcorn. The nice score of a goal and two tries against Ft. Helens nil was regietered.

div.head: EDUCA.TEONAL DEADLOCK AT
div.p: THE EDUCA.TEONAL DEADLOCK AT
BA R.NTOY.
CO-OPERATION OF SIR JOEIN BR!NNER AND THE BISHOP OF CHE'=tER.

On Thursday night a meeting of the inhabitants of Barnton,near Northwich, was held tor the purpose of re- ceiving from Sir John T. Brunner, M P.' a sch eme under which the educational deadlock which exists will be ended. Mr. Algernon Fletcher explained that the doctor had r.fused to allow Sir John to,leave the honse,and that the member for Northwich had required him to submit a statement. This set forth that throughout the agita- tion in Barnton, Sir John Brunner had fought for two objects—the first that the education given in Barnton should be improved,and the second that Nonconformist children should not, as now, be compelled to attend a Church of England school. During the past few weeks he had been in communication with the Bishop of Ches- ter, in the hope that some amicable arrangement might be concluded which would safeguard the educational interests and the religious liberties of Nonconformists. He (Sir John) wished to express in public his admiration of the spirit of tolerance which the Bishop had displayed throughout the negotiations The Bishop had given a ready and sympathetic consideration to the claims of the children of Nonconformists which he had urged, and the Bishop had also shown a genuine appreciation of his (Sir Jol,n Brunner's) anxiety that education at B —nton shou:d be improve . As a result of these nego- tiations the Bishop and he ha l agreed to a scheme— namely, that the present national school should nut be enlarged, and that the deficiency should be provided by Sir John building a r^'lool for 150 places. This new school was to be fitted in the best possible way. An ex- cellent playground would be provided, and for that pur- pose he (Sir John) proposed to ask Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co. to give an acre of ground, a request which he had no doubt would be granted. The school would be undenominational, and would supply the wants of those children who at preset] received no religious in- struction at all, or of a kind of which their parents dis- approved. No religious qcalifications would be necessary for service on the staff, and ic was believed that the school would contribute largely to the diminution of religious bitterness in local life. The school would be voluntary,and the Bishop's agreement to the scheme was conditional upon the withdrawal of the application for the formation of a school board. In advising this course Sir John felt that he was in no way sacrificing the principle which he and other friends of the school board system had advocated ; but he felt that it was impossible to expect the Department to consent to the formation of a Board. Sath.ied that it was absolutely hopeless to expect a school board, he was of opinion that they should be satisfied with the scheme described. As to the national school, he believed it would benefit by the change,and a great body of prejudice and illwill which was attached to such a school would be removed land religious bitterness and animosity done away with. ' The feeling of the meeting was that.had it been possible, a school board should have been formed; but it was clearly explained that as the'Education Department had granted permission to the Church party to extend their schools, they would not have recognised a new unds- neminational school. It was resolved,after considerable discussion, to accept Sir John Brunner's offer. There were only three dissentients.
NEWTON ITRBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL

A meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday afternoon. Mr. C. B.F. Borron. J.P., C.C., presided, and there were also present Rev.E. W. W. Kaye,Dr. Fatterson,Messrs.Collingwood,Emmett, McMahon, Gilmour, Stone, Simpson, Thompson Slee, Evans, Ormond, Beatty, Wood, with Mr. Shirley (Clerk), Mr. Worsley (law clerk), aild Mr. Brierley (surveyor).

At the meeting of the Cemetery Committee the Chair- man brought forward the question of clergymen's fees at the Cemetery being collected by the Cemetery keeper; and after a discussion thereon, the matter was deferred for further consideration.—The minutes of this commit- tee were approved of without further comment on the motion of the Rev. E. W. W. Kaye.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE

The School Attendance Officer's quarterly statement of attendance for the qu.rter ended, September 30th, showed that the total number on the books in nor various schools, with the exception of the Roman Catholic Schools where the information was refused, was 3,575 as compared with 2.632 in September, 189 b. The average attendance was 2,200 in comparison with 2.265 in the corresponding period last year.—Mr. McMahon remarked on the vacant places in the schools of the district. He found on looking through the blue book that they had room for 700 children more than at present. There were a great number of children walking about the streets who ought to be in the schools. He asked whether the School Attendance Committee was doing its duty, or was it a matter of form that there was a School Attendance Cern- mittee P—Mr. Ormind : Is this a matter which the Chairman has had due notice of P—Mr. McMahon raid it was only that day that he had a Chance of tool- og into the matter.—The Chairman: No notice has been given of the matter.—Mr. McMahon : It is none the less a fact. —Mr. Ormand said he did not wish to dispute Mr. McMahon's facts because Le did not carry blue books with him. But he thought it was inadvisable to enter into a discussion as to the accommodation in the schools of the district. It was a matter which should be very properly considered in coMmittee. He believed Mr. McMahon was a member of the School Census Commit- tee.—Mr. McMahon said that committee had nothing whatever to do with the subject of school attendance.— The Chairman said: it wa,s a matter which ought to be, and would he threshed out by the sub-committee which had been appointed. A census was being taken which would show the number of children in the neighbourhood and those attending schools. As regarded the work of that committee Ire could assure the Council that the Chairman was J. working chairman, and had ,given. the question a great deal of attention for many months. (Hear, hear.) The subject then dropped, and the minutes were passed

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Watkins (Nledical Officer of Health) in his quarterly report stated that during the quarter code LSeptember 30th, there were registered, births, 62 male 1. I 72 females, total 134 ; deaths, 21 male, 23 females.total 44 ; excess of births, 90. The birth rate Was 37'6 per thousand, and the death rate 123 per thousand of the estimated population. The infantile death rate was at an annnal rate of 123 per cent. The deaths of children under five years of aga were 454 per cent, of the total number of deaths. The diseases were—diptheria 1, cholera nostras ',whooping cough I,diarrhcea(choleraic) 1, rheumatic fever. phthisis 2, pulmonary diFeases 6, heart disease 4. injuries 1, other causes, 26. Neither of the choleraic cases was'notified, nor was the dur itien of the disease certified. There was no other death from diarrhceal disease certified. The zymotic sick rate (for the quarter) was 44 per thousand, being the heaviest experienced since the Notification Act was adopted, January, 1890. The several infectious cases notified were scarlatina 56, diphtheria 3, puerperal fever 1, erysipelas 3. total 63, aud their distribution was as follows :—Viaduct ward, 15; Town Hall ward, 21 ; Crow-'ane ward. 9 ; Wargrave ward. 5; Newton ward, 13 ; total, 63.. Fartueately the scarlatinal invasion was ef a mild type, as was demonstrated by only one fatal rase out of the 63 notified, and it was not improbable that there were many cmes that did not come under medical observation. Fortunately also, they were able to avail themselves of a greater amount of isolation than heretofore, 31 out of the 63 cases having bean sen to hospital. It was quite possible that the mildness of the type explained by tbe indifference and carelessness it engendered, the comparatively wider % dissemination of the disease than hitherto. PRECAUTIONS IN CASES OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES.

• The Highways, Public Works and Sanitary Commit- tee recommended that the schoolmasters in the district be notified by the Inspector of Nuisances of all infecti- ous cases, with a request that all the children ;n an infected house be kept away from school until ti thte- ment of the disease; and further, that the inhabitant. generally be informed that disinfectants may be ob- tained free of charge upon application to the Inspector of Nuisances at his office, Town Ball, Emlestown (Tam- worth-3t. entrance), between the hours of 9 0 a.m. and 10.0 a.m., and 5.0 p.m. to 5.30 p.m., and also upon application to the caretaker, Town Hal!, Newton, at any reasonable hour.

div.head: MISCELLANEOTJS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOTJS.

The Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Commit- tee also recommended that legal proceedings be taken against Henry Plant, of 21, Grafton-st., Earlestown, for keeping an unregistered common lodgine-house in con- travention of the Public Health Act, 1875; the Clerk as instructed at the last meeting of the committe produced counsel's opinion as to the powers of the Council to col- lect tolls on Newton Common, whereupon it was re- solved that the Chairman, the Clerk, and Mr. Worsley corfer with reference thereto and mate a statement thereon at the next meeting: that the surveyor furnish to this committee a monthly report of 811 the work done in his department from month to month, showing the various work done on the highways and streets, and to name any particular work which in his opinion may require to be done with the consent of the committee, , and such other information as it may be found necessary from time to time to embody in such:report;that the plan of two houses proposed to be built in Wargrave New Road by Mr. J. S. Eddhogton be approved and passed. The Surveyor was director te enquire (and report to the committe,) into a case which had come to the knowledge of the committee, of certain houses within the district having been built with the division walls between the bedrooms only 3 inches thick instead of 41 inches ; it was resolved that in future all building plans submitted to the committee must show figured dimensions of the thickness of the walls ; that Mr.Collingwood,Mr.Borron, Mr. Slee, and Mr. Beatty be, and they are hereby ap- pointed, a sub-committee to consider the advisability or otherwise of adopting the model bye-laws or of amend- ding the bye-!aws which are at present in force. Corres- pondence from Mr. Pardey (Lord Newton's agent) with reference to the improvement of Emmett's Brow was submitted, stating that he could not agree to the prc- posal to dispense with a retaining wall.—After consider- able discussion thereon it was resolved that the Clerk be empowercd to write to Lord Newton's agent stating that the committee have fully considered the matter, and suggest that he agree to the original scheme ; especially considering that the land proposed to be acquired for the improvement of Emmett's Brow is,in the opinion of this committee, public land, and that it is proposed to proceed with the work according to the original plan. Mr. W. Collingwood moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Gilmour wished to know why a resolution of the committee had been omitted. He brought the Aubject of the paving of Common-road before the commlttee,and it was resolved that the surveyor should furnish a report showing the cost which had been incurred. If he allowed the minutes to pass without mentioning the matter he would be told at the next meeting of the Council that there was no minute. It was a very important matter and he contendod that their Surveyor had no right to make four or five hundred yards of street without the sanction of the committee.—The Chairman in reply said he had no recollection of the matter having been brought for- ward at the committee. If Mr. Gilmour desired infor- mation for the committee,the Surveyor would provide it for the next meeting.—Mr. Gilmour said Mr. Stone se- conded his proposition in committee. He thought the public should know what the cost had been.—Mr. Stone said he had not the slightest recollection of such a reso- lution that ts Surveyor should furnish the committee with the cost of Common road. It was decided that the Surveyor should keen an account of the cost of the vari- ous repairs of roads and streets going on,so that he could furnish them wit the cost when asked to do so.—The Chairman said s h information as Mr. Gilinour desired was quite proper and correct, but the Clerk had nothing in his minutes showing that any decision was come to by the committee respecting it. There must have been some slight omission, but the Surveyor would furnish the information asked for at the next meeting of the committee.—Mr. Gilmour said he , would give notice that the Surveyor be instructed to fur- nish the information asked for at the next meeting of Use committee.—Mr. Gilmour said he would give notice that the Surveyor be instructed to furnish the cost of , the paving of Common-road.—The subject then dropped. j —The Chairman said he would like to allude to the very favourable position in which that district stood in regard to the death rate. He had been looking at the County ' return, for the quarter-ending September 30th, and he j found that the general average of death rate in County districts was 154 whilst the Newton district was 98 per thousand. He thought that was a very low death rate, and he did not think there was one urban distriet that touched it at all. Such a position of affairs was very satisfactory indeed.—Mr. Gilmour alluded to the large number of children being taken to the Fever ward, and said the prevalence of disease was very serious. He was not surprised at it. considering their filthy streets. All sorts ef garbage was allowed to remain in the atreets,and the stench from the gullies and manholes was frightful. He felt certain that if some stringent measures were not taken in sanitary matters they would have an epidemic. —The Chairman said the Surveyor had already notified the owners of streets who had not got them paved that ' they must abate in some way the nuisanees of standing water in the street and other causes. Many had replied saying the matter would he attended to, and he did not think there was any necessity to discuss the matter there.—Mr. Gilmour complained that " stuff" was tipped into some streets without being spread.—The minutes were then passed. GAS MANAGER'S REPORT.

Mr. Joseph Swann in his report to the Chairman of the Gas and Water Committee said the .extension of the street lamps was now completed as far as instruction, received, and the number of new lamps fixed during this summer and autumn was as follows :—Park Road Newton, 14, Southworth Road, Newton, 9, Wargrave Road, 8, Booth-st., Earlestown, 2, Chandcs-st., 2, Lawrence-st., 2, Newton Terrace. 2, Queen-st , 1, Rath- bone-st., 2, Regent-ot., 2, total, 44. They had fixed two lame incandescent lamps, one at the corner of Bridge-ot., and one at the bottom of Queen-ot. ; also all the lamps in Bridge-at., Queen-st., and Market-st. had been altered to the incandescent light, the number of these lights now in use was viz.: Newton 2, Wargrave 2, Earlestown 27, total 31. During the late storms they P ad had a little trouble with the inc-.ndescentlights,but with some altera- tions ts the old lamps, it co Id te obviated in the future. The demand for automatic meters was still maintained, during the past five weeks they had fixed upwards of fifty,and they had over fifty more applications for them, but the emit of meters of that description was again exhausted. Since the price of coke was lowered the sales had iacreised and the stock reduced a little.lf was important that he (Mr. Swami) should be at the Gas Works between five and six in the evening, . when the men were changing from day work to night syork,eopec- ially during the winter months,a.nd he should be obliged if it can be so arranged as to have the committee meet- ings held earlier. The consumption of water-during the month ot September, was :—Newton Bridge meter 8,160,000 gallons, Viaduct 1,920,000 gallons, Park Side 5,090 total 5,085,000 gallons ; corresponding month I at year 4,862,000 gallons, increase 423,000 gal- lons.—The committee resolved that the Chairmen of the severe committees—Mr. Barron, Mr. Collingwood, Mr. Ormand, Mr. Wood, and Rev. E. W. W. Kaye—forrn a sub-committee to consider the question of there-arrange- ment of the order and time of holding the usual month-11y meetings of the respective committees of the 6)unciloio as to allow of the gas manager being at the Gas Works between the hours of five and six o'clock in the evening as mentioned in the report —The recommendation was adopted.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr. Ormand moved the adoption of the minute 4 of the Finance Committee which contained a resolution that the Council obzain a loan of £2OOO for gas distribu- ton on security of the gas works and that the offer of Parr's Bank Limited to loan the same at a favourable rate of interest to be repaid in five equal instalmenta of principal and interest be accepted.—Mr. Stone seconded and the minutes were adopted.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. The Clerk read a supplementary report of the Fire Appliances Committee as follows :—Resolved, that a suitable box (portable) with a glass front and slauting roof be ordered and fixed near to the Police Station,War- grave, and that Mr. Swann see to the carrying out of this resolution. Mr. Collingwood to be requested to fly upon the exact spot ; that Mr. Swann, Gas Manager, be superint,ndent of the Fire Brigade, and that he be lheld responsible for proper care being taken of the stand pipes, hose, &c.,and that the men practice once a month as fixed by the superinteDdent ; that the names of Vr, workmen now submitted be requested to act aq firemen, and that the Gas Manager and Surveyor be respectively instructed to inform their men (as ger nameitsubmittod) that they are required to act as firemen in case of tiFe •, and that a requisite uumber of plates with the word " Fireman "thereon be ordered and affixed to the resid- ences of the firemein. The Clerk was directed to write to the Inspector of Police, asking him to be good enough to instruct the men under his charge„ to report to the Gas Manager any damage to street hydrants that may come under their notice.—The report wa9 adopted on the proposition of the Chairman. EA.RLESTOWN AND DISTRICT WOMEN'S LIDERA. ASSOCIATION.

The monthly meeting!' of the above Association was held on Monday in the Co-operative Hall,when about 50 members were present. The meeting opened with a short address from the President, Mrs. Rawlins of Raiuhill, on the benefits of educa- tion• after which along, interesting, and instructive prfp-i* was read by Miss Allatt on the "Origin of. National Schools." An animated discussion then followed in which Mrs. Rawlins, Miss Watson and other members took part, explaining, the difference between the voluntary and Board School system of education, and the members were urged to obtain still further knowledge ou the education question as another Bill bearing on this sUbject may be ex- pec..ed to be brought forward at the next Parlia- mentary session. A vote of thanks to Miss Allatt was proposed by Miss Greenall, seconded and sup- ported. Tea was then handed round and thus closed this interesting meeting. The next meeting will take place on Monday, December 7th, when a paper will be read by Mrs. Miller.
